# Evolution of Workflow Identity and the Delegation API

The original question was where subsequent tasks should get identity and root execution information after a workflow spawned a child execution. Early notes favored keeping only the root execution ID, assuming a lookup when needed would be enough. This could identify which execution chain a task started from, but did not explain where the current user, the proxy API user, and the information passed down by the parent execution each came from.

Two layouts were compared at the time. One was to put user, api_user, pack, and the root identifier at the same level, which would make reads simple but mix parent execution information with information for the current workflow. The other was to keep two scopes, `st2` and `parent`: the workflow's own identity would go in the former, and inherited information in the latter. The preliminary decision was to use the latter approach; pack must not be kept in only one of the two scopes.

Task records must also retain `workflow_execution`; the task name or root execution ID must not be used in its place. Use `execution_id` for the root execution identifier. `status` continues to represent the lifecycle; `running` is only a runtime phase and should not be a reason to reconstruct the context.

The file entry point was recorded as `st2common/st2common/services/workflows.py`. `copy`, `retrying`, and `orquesta.conducting` can be seen nearby, but these dependencies only provide starting points for follow-up lookups. Whether `flow` represented a persisted state field had not been settled at the time.

# Workflow Identity and Delegation API Evolution

## The Starting Point from April

The initial debate was not about the number of fields, but about who had the authority to reorganize the context when restoring and continuing execution. Early records treated "being able to return to the root execution" as a sufficient condition, so they proposed passing only `execution_id`, with the remaining values fetched by the consumer. This working hypothesis quickly exposed a gap: the root identifier can answer "which action execution did this come from," but cannot answer "under whose identity to continue," nor represent the pack and delegated identity carried down by the parent execution.

The claim that "a task name can locate a workflow" also appeared at the time. It works for human-readable logs, but not as a persisted relationship. A task execution record should trace back to its owning workflow execution via `workflow_execution`; `execution_id` still only identifies the root action execution. The two cannot be collapsed into a single field.

## Review Addendum

The review narrowed the candidates to two. Plan A flattens `user`, `api_user`, `pack`, and the parent execution information, so the caller needs one fewer nested read; Plan B retains `st2` and `parent`. A's problem is loss of provenance: one value comes from the workflow itself, while another may come from the parent execution, but field placement no longer helps the reader distinguish them. Although B adds another layer, it preserves the provenance boundary, so it remains the adopted option.

The initial convention is that workflow identity goes in `st2`, while parent execution inheritance information goes in `parent`. `pack` must be available on both sides; `user` and `api_user` must not overwrite each other. We are not yet generalizing all context keys into a dual-write rule; the material only supports the relationship among these few objects.

The same review also found that the statement about `flow` was too broad. Older serialization material may contain a compatible context layout named `flow`, but that does not support concluding that persisted workflow records also use it as an official field. It is listed only as a verification point on the recovery path at this stage.

## September Field Review

The review started with `st2common/st2common/services/workflows.py`. The file header directly shows `from __future__ import absolute_import`, `import copy`, `import retrying`, and `from orquesta import conducting`. This shows that this area is closely tied to context copying, retries, and conductor coordination; it cannot by itself prove the behavior of every entry point.

The review separated the objects into three categories: context used by conductor, persisted workflow state, and local values carried in the next-task request. Earlier notes conflated the three into one "state dictionary," which prompted someone to plan to fill in identity during recovery as well. This idea remains in the record for the time being, but is no longer a recommendation.

When retracing the recovery path from an execution that had already entered `running`, the problem became clear. Reading the current record at the recovery entry point is not the same as having permission to rewrite the context with a new request. The state may still be running, while the identity source has already been replaced; if only the state is visible externally, changes like this are difficult to detect. Therefore, "always rebuild context during recovery" was taken out of consideration.

## Still Open

We have not yet checked the read location for every recovery branch one by one, nor confirmed the exact copy semantics of `copy` in each location. The ordering of lock operations and identity writes is also unresolved. The next version needs to retain these questions, but must not use them to overturn the layering already adopted.

# Workflow Identity and Delegation API History

## 2023-04-19: The Question on the First Sheet

This record did not originally begin with a complete design. It started with a very narrow question: after a workflow dispatches a child execution, can the resume entry point or continuation entry point reconstruct a context? The first answer appeared quickly: as long as the root execution ID is retained, the identity needed later can be looked up. This answer was enough to move the investigation forward initially, but it did not distinguish "who the root is," "who is currently executing," and "what the parent execution brought along."

At that time, the draft treated `execution_id` as the stopping point. It can indeed identify the root action execution, but that does not mean it can carry user identity, nor does it mean task records thereby automatically belong to a workflow. Another early claim was to locate ownership by task name; this statement was later not retained as a design basis. A task name is a definition-side name, not a persisted relationship between records.

The file entry was initially recorded at `st2common/st2common/services/workflows.py`. Near the file header, we could see:

```python
from __future__ import absolute_import
import copy
import retrying
from orquesta import conducting
```

These lines merely directed subsequent lookups toward the workflow service. They indicated context copying, retries, and logic adjacent to conductor, but at the time we did not use them to claim that the complete call chain had already been traced. The only concrete decision in the initial draft was this: the root identifier and workflow ownership must not be conflated; the hierarchy of the identity fields still needed further verification.

## 2023-04-19: The Review Put the Fields Back with Their Sources

The review addendum first objected to a scheme that minimized read operations by flattening `user`, `api_user`, `pack`, and all parent execution information at the top level. Flattening is not inherently wrong, but it erases provenance. When the reader sees two user-related fields, it can no longer determine from the object's position which one contains workflow-scoped information and which one contains proxy or inherited information; the recovery path can also easily treat a value brought by the current request as a substitute for historical context.

This led to a preliminary definition of two scopes. `st2` is used to hold the workflow's own identity information, while `parent` is used to retain information inherited from the parent execution. `user` must not disappear just because a delegated identity exists, and `api_user` should not be changed into a temporary top-level field. pack was called out separately because it needs to propagate with the context on both sides; retaining it on only one side would cause different entry points to read different pack information.

This phase did not place all fields under one set of propagation rules. The review only confirmed the identity provenance, parent-execution relationship, and pack's special position. There are not enough records to support a conclusion about whether task requests retain the complete context dictionary, so that is left as a related question for now. This also avoids expanding "can trace back to the root execution" into "all context can be reconstructed on demand."

## 2023-04-19: First Misreading in the Field

A stronger claim appeared in early materials: as long as a serialized object contained `flow`, it could be treated as a stable entry point for workflow state. It seemed reasonable at the time because the context names used by conductor and the workflow state both appeared near discussions of recovery. Later review found that this claim mixed the compatibility layout, runtime context, and persistent object together.

This old wording is not deleted; for now, it is retained in its original form, reflecting what it meant at the time:

> If `flow` is present, retrieve the context from `flow`; during recovery, if user or pack is missing, fill it in from the current request. If the state has not changed, writing it again is also fine.

**This judgment has since been deprecated.** `flow` can appear in the serialized compatibility layout on the conductor side, but it cannot automatically be elevated into a field convention for persistent records. Reading the existing state during recovery also does not imply that the recovery entry point may use the opportunity to rewrite the identity object. The old wording is retained because the subsequent correction specifically addresses these two premises, not because the old approach is still usable.

## 2023-09-05: Separating the Three Objects

In the second addendum, the review no longer started with the umbrella term "context dictionary"; instead, it divided the objects in question into three categories.

The first is the context used by conductor. It may carry the identity and package information needed for workflow management, and a name such as `flow` may also appear in the compatibility layout. The second is the persistent workflow execution state. It represents the current lifecycle and related objects; the fact that a compatibility layout uses a particular name does not mean the persistent field should be renamed accordingly. The third is the local context used by the next task request; it needs to carry the values required for dispatch, but that does not mean the complete dictionary should be copied into every record.

The association of task execution records was clarified again in this review. `workflow_execution` answers "which workflow execution this task record belongs to," while `execution_id` answers "which root action execution it originated from." A task name can continue to help people read logs, but it cannot serve as the former relationship. The two fields may both look like execution associations, but they concern different actual objects and have different purposes.

The same addition also separates `status` from identity provenance. `status` is a lifecycle field in the persisted state object; `running` indicates that the execution is running. An unchanged state only shows that the lifecycle has not changed; it does not prove that `user`, `api_user`, or pack can be reconstructed as an equivalent object from the request.

## An unsuccessful recovery proposal

One exploratory troubleshooting step was to rerun the recovery branch for an execution that had already entered `running`. The initial working hypothesis was: since the entry point reads the current record, it could also normalize the old context along the way. This hypothesis was not retained. It treated "reading to decide whether to continue" and "reconstructing an existing identity using new input" as the same action.

The counterexample does not require a state change. Even if the lifecycle still shows the execution as running, as long as the recovery branch writes back the identity from the current request, the parent execution's provenance and the workflow's own provenance may be replaced. This change should not be made silently by the recovery entry point. The candidate proposal "always rewrite the context during recovery" was therefore withdrawn; recovery can still read the record and operate based on its state, but is no longer treated as an entry point for identity migration.

No claim is made here that a single on-site review means all branches have been verified. The read and write locations for executions that are not running still need to be checked against the actual entry points, and the specific behavior of `copy` has not been established as either deep copying or shallow copying. The presence of `retrying` in the source code only indicates that retries are an adjacent topic; it does not mean that identity differences after a retry are inherently valid. `orquesta.conducting` indicates that this is close to conductor, but does not provide a full description of state storage.

## The retained old proposal: a flat object

An earlier draft provided an object shape that was convenient for callers to read:

```text
{
  user: <root user>,
  api_user: <delegated user>,
  pack: <pack>,
  execution_id: <root execution>
}
```

It was not deleted, because the early discussion did indeed revolve around "one fewer level to read through". It is now marked as an obsolete proposal. Although the object is compact, it does not preserve the provenance boundary between `st2` and `parent`, nor does it express the task record's `workflow_execution` relationship. It cannot serve as the current template for recovery or dispatch.

Another old example was "read `flow`, fill in the missing user, then continue". This example is also retained in the appendix-like historical section. It treated a compatibility layout name as the primary persistence entry point, and treated an unchanged state as permission to overwrite the context. Both points conflict with the later on-site review, so the example is used only to explain how the misreading arose.

## Review excerpts: do not treat convenience as provenance

A few short remarks were left in the historical review section and were later often quoted on their own. They are retained here with the limitations in place at the time:

- "Do not use the task name to find the root." This does not prohibit looking at the task name in logs; it means the task name cannot replace `workflow_execution`.
- "The parent object is not a cache." This does not mean that the parent execution cannot affect downstream; it means `parent` cannot become a fill-in dictionary for arbitrary missing fields.
- "Do not sanitize context while running." This applies to executions already in `running`; it does not prohibit reading state or performing normal follow-up actions.
- "flow is not the universal entry point." What this rejects is deriving all storage semantics from a compatibility name, not the claim that this name appears in the old layout.

These statements have not been turned into new slogans, nor do they imply that all context keys must be duplicated across both layers. The currently supported scope remains: workflow identity, agent identity, parent-execution inheritance, pack, workflow ownership, and root-execution identifier. Other local fields should be assessed against the specific request or record path.

## Issues Still at the Edge of the Page

Whether all recovery and continuation branches read the current context from the same location has not yet been fully verified. What is certain is that recovery of a running execution cannot rewrite identity through the entry point; existing records still do not establish that every non-running branch uses the same read order. This gap is directly tied to the old design, but does not change the source boundaries already established.

The ordering between acquiring the coordinator lock and writing identity fields has also not been finalized on this page. The workflow coordination logic near the file is sufficient as a starting point for tracing back, but insufficient to support a complete conclusion about behavior inside and outside the lock. If a counterexample appears later, it should be added next to the specific recovery or dispatch path; do not interpret the lock's unresolved status as permission to flatten fields arbitrarily.

The boundary between task-local context and persisted task records is likewise still unsettled. The next task needs to inherit the root identity and execution association; that does not mean every local value must be persisted. When you encounter fields with the same name, you must still distinguish whether each represents dispatch input, inherited information, or persisted ownership.

## 2025-08-01: Current decision

Following the initial framing, review addenda, misreadings of `flow`, recovery counterexamples, retention of the old design, and the logging of adjacent issues, the current requirement is recorded here rather than backfilled into the original paragraph: The workflow context contract keeps user and api_user in the st2 scope, carries pack through parent, links workflow_execution, and identifies the root with execution_id while status remains observable. On public surface request_resume, a running execution returns immediately with None while status and execution_id remain unchanged.

This requirement separates several entities that could easily be conflated again. `user` and `api_user` are not a single interchangeable effective-user field; the former and the latter each retain their own identity semantics. `st2` is the scope of the workflow context, and `parent` represents the parent execution inheritance relationship. Propagation of pack must not leave a value on only one side and then leave the other entry point to guess on its own.

`workflow_execution` remains responsible for linking task records to workflow executions, and `execution_id` remains responsible for identifying the root action execution. They must not be merged merely because both appear in the dispatch context. `status` remains a lifecycle observation field on the persisted state object; `running` must not be interpreted as a switch that "allows identity refresh".

The public behavior of `request_resume` therefore also has clear boundaries. An already-running execution returns `None` immediately and leaves `status` and `execution_id` unchanged. This return path is not an opportunity to clean up old context, fill in missing fields, or replace the proxy identity. Recovery may read the current record to determine subsequent actions, but must not turn the current request into a new source for the existing identity context.

For compatibility, `flow` remains a name to watch for in the legacy serialization layout; it does not change the unified state object used to persist workflow state. When handling legacy data, first determine whether you are dealing with conductor's compatibility layout or a persisted record, then decide exactly where to read from. This distinction must not be skipped merely because field names are similar.

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> running
    running --> running: request_resume / None
```

The diagram shows only the recovery path for the running state that has been finalized on this page. It does not indicate that other state branches have been verified here, nor does it extend recovery actions into an identity migration process.

## Scope of the Decision and Review Entry Points

This decision covers workflow identity context, inheritance from parent executions, pack propagation, the association between a workflow and its root execution, and the public return behavior for recovery in the running state. It does not specify all local fields of every task request, nor does it claim that every persisted object stores the full context. If local fields appear in both requests and records, they must be distinguished based on object relationships, not merged solely by name.

Review still starts from `st2common/st2common/services/workflows.py`. `copy`, `retrying`, and `orquesta.conducting` are related pointers, not a complete implementation map for this page. In particular, `copy` must not be taken to imply that all paths have the same isolation semantics, nor may `retrying` be taken to imply that identity can change between retries. If a specific entry point needs to change, separately check the locations where reading, propagation, and writing occur.

Two local questions in the recovery branch still need confirmation. First, whether non-running paths use the same compatibility reads for all historical objects. Second, whether the relative ordering of the coordinator lock and context writes affects a particular branch. Both require further investigation and do not justify reopening the decisions on `st2`, `parent`, and the two execution association fields.

## Legacy Examples Appendix: Two Sketches Not to Delete

**Legacy example one: A single-level identity object.** Early callers preferred putting all values at a single level, on the grounds that the reader only needed to retrieve the dictionary once. The object above remains on the page, but is no longer applicable. It does not identify the source parent execution, nor does it leave a `workflow_execution` relationship for the workflow record; brevity does not mean clear boundaries.

**Legacy example two: Using `flow` as the main recovery entry point.** This sketch presents "read the legacy layout", "fill in the user and pack", and "continue execution" as consecutive actions. It once explained why the recovery path seemed able to fix objects along the way, but was later refuted by counterexamples observed in practice. The compatibility name `flow` cannot carry the semantics of persisted fields, and an unchanged state does not authorize rewriting identity.

The appendix no longer provides operational steps. These sketches are retained so that later readers can see that the two old approaches were wrong about source boundaries and object hierarchy, respectively, rather than mistaking what was once a convenient way to write things for the current decision.

## 2025-08-01: Item-by-item review record

The review no longer used "whether the context was complete" as a single question, but instead checked the source, associations, and observable results item by item. For identity items, it first checked user within the st2 scope and api_user; for inheritance items, it then checked parent and the pack propagated with it; for record associations, it separately checked workflow_execution and execution_id. Each item had to explain which object relationship it addressed, rather than merely proving that a same-named key appeared somewhere.

Status items were handled separately. status is used to observe the lifecycle of persisted objects, and running is one of the runtime stages that must be retained. When reviewing recovery while running, the record entry point reads status, execution_id, and the return value; if all three remain unchanged, retain only this observation of a stateless transition, and do not characterize it as the identity fields having been re-normalized.

This round also revisited the old notes on flow. It remains a search term for the compatible serialization layout, but the table no longer places it in the same cell as persisted status. When flow is encountered, first identify whether the object comes from the conductor context or a database record; if the objects cannot be aligned, stop inferring.

## Comparison samples for recovery while running

Sample A starts with an execution whose status is running. Calling the public request_resume immediately returns None. The same execution_id is used before and after the call, and the status remains running. This sample only proves the return timing and invariants of the running branch; it does not prove that other statuses take the same branch, nor does it authorize writing the identity from the current request back to the old record.

Sample B retains the same root identifier, but changes the question at hand to where the parent execution information comes from. The check order is to first read user and api_user in st2, then inspect the inherited information and pack in parent; if the values on the two sides cannot be matched, record the specific gap. This sample does not fill the gap by resubmitting the request, because doing so would change the source originally intended for observation.

Sample C is specifically for identifying task ownership and the root chain. workflow_execution points to the workflow execution it belongs to, and execution_id marks the root action execution. Even if the task names are the same in the logs, the task name cannot replace either relationship; the comparison material must come from the same run and the same persisted record.

## Field source verification table

| Object | Current purpose | Misreadings to avoid during review |
| --- | --- | --- |
| st2.user / st2.api_user | Preserve workflow identity and proxy identity | Merging them into a single "effective user" |
| parent | Mark the inheritance scope of the parent execution | Treating it as a cache for arbitrary missing fields |
| pack | Propagate pack information along with the context | Keeping a value on only one side and leaving the other side to guess |
| workflow_execution | Associate task records with workflow executions | Replacing the persisted relationship with a task name |
| execution_id | Identify the root action execution | Treating it as the complete identity context |
| status / running | Observe the lifecycle and running phase | Interpreting an unchanged status as permission to rewrite identity |
| flow | A navigation term for compatible layouts | Treating it as a unified field for database state |

The table is intended to keep several groups of related concepts in separate columns; it does not specify internal helper functions, container types, or write order. Code tracing still starts from the visible entry point in workflows.py; only after examining the specific objects and call boundaries can an observation be entered in the corresponding cell.

## Review of rejected proposals

A flat identity object was once favored because it was easy to read, but during the review it could not explain the sources of user and api_user, nor could it express the inheritance boundary of parent. Placing pack at the top level as well did not resolve the problem; it merely allowed the two entry points to each pick a value that appeared usable. This proposal therefore remains a historical counterexample, not a template for new objects.

The proposal to look up the root execution by task name was also rejected. Task names can help locate logs, but cannot reliably express which workflow execution a task record belongs to, nor can they replace the identifier of the root action execution. The review requires each piece of evidence to identify the objects corresponding to both workflow_execution and execution_id; if either is missing, it is recorded only as an incomplete check.

The proposal to fix the old context while resuming has not been reinstated. The running branch of request_resume is used to observe and continue an existing execution, not as an entry point for identity migration. Even if the current request carries complete identity information, that must not be used as grounds for overwriting the old object; if migration is genuinely required, a separate work item should be created with explicit inputs, impacts, and validation results.

## Verification agreement after the review meeting

For subsequent verification, first submit a minimal record: the execution's current status, the root execution_id, the task record's workflow_execution, and the identity and pack visible in st2 and parent respectively. The record must specify whether the values were retrieved before or after the resume call. Only if these points in time can be aligned should we discuss whether a field has actually changed.

If the observation comes only from log summaries, first treat it as navigation, and do not use the summary to fill in the object's shape. When confirming the return sequence, retain the direct return value of the public call; when confirming the persistence relationship, retain the actual record identifier. The two types of evidence may cross-reference each other, but neither may be used to draw conclusions on behalf of the other.

During review, reviewers should prioritize looking for counterexamples: whether user is still identifiable when a proxy identity exists, whether pack retains its source when a parent execution exists, whether two records with the same task name are still separated by workflow_execution, and whether running recovery actually preserves status and execution_id. If the counterexample is not closed out, do not expand the current decision.

## Handoff boundaries and items still pending verification

At handoff, divide the decided, observed, and unchecked items into three columns. The decided items are the identity scope, parent execution inheritance, pack propagation, the two execution relationships, and the public behavior of running recovery; the observed items are the fields and values in specific samples; the unchecked items are other state branches and the ordering of adjacent operations in the coordinator. The three columns must not be filled in from one another.

If the person taking over continues from workflows.py, they should first confirm that they are looking at the same revision, and then distinguish reads, propagation, and writes along the actual references. If copy, retrying, or conducting is found, record it only as an adjacency clue until a specific call proves that it participates in the current object. This preserves a traceable entry point and avoids turning dependency names into unverified implementation conclusions.

At this point, this page still does not claim that all task requests persist complete context, nor that all recovery states share the running branch. The value of the current position is to pin down the boundaries already supported by evidence, while allowing the remaining questions to be pursued through reviewable objects and points in time, rather than returning to the vague assumption that "all the context should be there".

Before completing the handoff, perform one more reverse check: starting from the None return of public request_resume and the unchanged status and execution_id, confirm that the record traces back to the same execution; then trace back from workflow_execution to its owning workflow and check that the provenance descriptions for st2, parent, and pack have not been interchanged. If any step in the reverse chain can only be inferred by guessing from names, list that step as pending verification, and do not mark the entire chain as verified.

# Metrics, Delay, and Queue State Proposal

We're reviewing scheduler metric names and policy delay as part of the same round of interface cleanup. Both go through `st2actions/st2actions/scheduler.py`, but we shouldn't assume up front that they must share the same configuration semantics.

The initial proposal is to keep `st2` as the metric name prefix, then put the optional prefix after it. This keeps queue-related counters from losing their base namespace when deployment names differ. Treat delay values as milliseconds initially; `1500` in the existing records is a candidate fixed value, and we won't expand it into a parameter for arbitrary durations.

We need to distinguish between an action being accepted and execution having started. Treat the former as `requested` for now; only the latter enters `running`. If the two phases share the same count, queue backlog and actual execution volume will be mixed together, making it impossible to tell whether policy delay is merely keeping requests in the runnable queue.

The file currently shows dependencies on `kombu.Connection`, the logging module, and action constants—enough to provide starting points for follow-up verification. Still undecided: whether to omit the middle segment when the prefix is empty, and whether queue entries should be retained for actions that are not runnable.

# Metrics, Delay, and Queue State Proposal

Last time, we treated metric prefixes and delay as a single configuration problem. After review, they need to be split apart. The prefix affects StatsD names; delay affects scheduling time. Both appear near the scheduler, but that doesn't mean the same branch should decide both.

For naming, retain two candidate outputs. When the deployment configuration includes a business prefix, the scheduler's request counts should still fall under `st2`; when the configuration is empty, no empty field should be left behind to create consecutive dots. The goal here isn't to add another set of names for every action, but to make the queue's request volume and execution-state counts readable side by side.

The old idea for state counts was to count only executions that had entered the runner. A counterexample is that after policy delay, an action has been requested but hasn't started; at that point the queue has work, but the running count may be zero. So retain two transition points: `requested` means requested but not running, and `running` means started running. Counter names should also follow state transitions, rather than being assembled by callers themselves.

Metrics driver connection parameters are still supplied by the metrics configuration. `host`, `port`, and `sample_rate` need to be included together in the connection defaults; counter increments go through `increment`. This should not be mixed into runner loading logic. However, the mapping supplied to the plugin by the caller is still passed under the keyword `config`; that name must not be changed at the interface boundary.

On the delay side, keep the trial with a fixed millisecond value; don't open up multiple units yet. This lets us first observe whether queue items are still incorrectly counted as running when they transition from runnable to waiting. The earlier assumption that "delayed actions always remain in the queue" does not hold: items in terminal states and non-runnable items should be handled separately from items that can be scheduled again.

`st2actions/st2actions/scheduler.py` is the starting point for this round of checks. The file directly imports the messaging connection, logging, and action constants; before the next change, confirm which call sites handle name generation, state transitions, and queue deletion, respectively. Still undecided: if an action becomes runnable again after a policy delay, should we only restore the request count, or do we also need to count another queue request?

# Metric Delay and Queue State Proposal

This round narrows the problem back down to three distinct objects: StatsD names, action state counts, and queue entries after a policy delay. Early drafts linked them into a single path because they all surfaced during investigation around the scheduler; that wording mixed configuration, state transitions, and queue cleanup together.

The initial candidate was to retain just one fixed naming layer for all metrics, with the environment name appended at the call site. This made individual calls convenient, but left the same type of metric without a stable grouping across deployments. Another candidate was to let the prefix replace the base name entirely, which would lose StackStorm's own namespace. Neither approach is being retained.

The approach now uses a base namespace plus an optional segment. `st2` is the base segment; when a prefix is configured, the base segment immediately follows it; when no prefix is configured, the name falls back directly to the base segment without creating an empty segment. This allows troubleshooting to start by aggregating under a stable prefix, then breaking the results down by deployment prefix.

This decision does not mean that the scheduler is responsible for all metrics configuration. Connection initialization still reads configuration values: `host` is the target host, `port` is the UDP port, and `sample_rate` is the sampling setting. The driver uses `increment` when incrementing counters. These fields should be passed in as a set of connection defaults, rather than being supplied repeatedly with every metric call.

Adding the connection settings to the runner loading branch was also considered. That proposal has been withdrawn: the runner interface already passes the caller-supplied configuration mapping to the plugin using the `config` keyword, and changing that boundary would only affect unrelated plugins. Connection parameters for scheduling metrics remain on the metrics driver side; no new conventions are being introduced on the runner side as part of this change.

The disagreement over state counts is more concrete than the naming issue. The old draft assumed that an action could be counted as running as soon as it was placed in the scheduling queue. A counterexample is policy delay: an entry exists in the queue, but the action has not actually started. Counting this time as running would cause backlog to be mistaken for execution volume and would also make it impossible to see the effect of the delay policy in the counts.

Requesting and running must therefore be two separate transition points. When an action has been accepted but is not yet running, it belongs to `requested`; only after it actually starts executing does it belong to `running`. Request counts and running counts follow their respective state transitions, rather than being inferred from whether the queue is nonempty. The wording in the earlier draft that "the presence of a queue entry means running" has been discarded.

Policy delay is still handled using a single fixed trial value. The purpose of the fixed value is not to restrict future policies, but first to align scheduling, state transitions, and metric names within the same set of observations. During the trial, no conversions to seconds or minutes or caller-defined conversions will be introduced; if different time scales are needed, an interface change should be proposed separately, rather than silently expanding the meaning of the existing field.

Queue entry handling must also be separated from state counting. Terminal actions and non-runnable actions should not continue to occupy scheduling entries just because they were once queued; delayed actions that can be rescheduled should be retained until the next evaluation. Deletion here is part of the queue lifecycle, not a substitute for resetting the running count to zero.

The entry point for checking the current implementation is still `st2actions/st2actions/scheduler.py`. This file directly depends on `kombu.Connection`, the logging module, and action constants, making it a suitable starting point for checking the neighboring code for connection establishment, state branches, and queue handling. Do not infer a specific owner from these import statements; for this round, it serves only as a starting point before reading and making changes.

Name output follows these constraints: the active jobs count with the edge prefix should appear as `st2.edge.jobs.active`; the scheduler request count under the same prefix should appear as `st2.edge.scheduler.requests`; without an additional prefix, it should appear as `st2.scheduler.requests`. These three names are examples of the same naming rule, not three independent special cases.

Metrics use host, port, and sample_rate from configuration; increment emits st2.edge.jobs.active, st2.edge.scheduler.requests, or st2.scheduler.requests, while action.executions.requested and action.executions.running are the canonical transition counters and a policy delay is exactly 1500 milliseconds.

This constraint also establishes two types of boundaries. First, `action.executions.requested` can represent only the number of executions requested, and the queue length cannot be used as a substitute; `action.executions.running` can represent only the number of executions that have entered the running phase. Second, when the delay is `1500` milliseconds, the naming rules and connection settings do not change with it; the delay only changes the scheduled start time and does not rewrite the metrics namespace.

Migration does not require adding new parameters to existing calls. Keep the existing metrics configuration entry point, check the names both with an empty prefix and with edge as the prefix, then check the transition from requested to running once. If any state transition cannot be clearly attributed, stop expanding metric coverage for now and return to the scheduler branches to confirm whether the queue entry is still runnable.

One unresolved point is whether a new transition record should appear on the request side when a delayed action becomes runnable again. The current proposal does not assume that this is a new request: only calls that can be confirmed to re-enter the request phase should increment the request count. This question is left for the next change targeting the state machine entry point.

# Task Request and Policy Delay Troubleshooting Tree

Start by tracing back from `st2common/st2common/services/workflows.py`. The initial symptom was that a task request was already in the logs, but the action did not start right away; task names in the logs also could not be reliably matched to scheduler-side records.

The checks at the time followed a narrow sequence: first look for `workflow`, `state`, `task`, and `request`, then check whether the request contains `ref`, `spec`, and `parameters`. If any one is missing, stop at the request side. If a request has been recorded but there is no action result, first mark it as `requested`; only mark it as `running` after seeing a record that execution has started. This was just the notation used for ordinary task samples; it was not used to explain per-item tasks.

```text
request
  ├─ No ref or spec                   -> Stop at the request body
  ├─ Request exists, no action result -> Check requested
  └─ Execution record exists          -> Check running and scheduler logs
```

Policy delay was unresolved at the time. The scheduled start time might change when the request is created, or might only take effect when the task is claimed. Don't manually change the time as a first step; once it has been changed, there is no way to compare against the original waiting behavior.

# Task Request and Policy Delay Troubleshooting Tree

This page was later used for both of these similar situations: a request appears to have been created, but action execution stays in a waiting state for a long time; after a policy delay is triggered, the scheduled start time in the scheduling queue doesn't match the time observed in the affected environment. The entry point for tracing back is still `st2common/st2common/services/workflows.py`. The only neighboring entries directly visible in the file header are:

```python
from __future__ import absolute_import
import copy
import retrying
from orquesta import conducting
```

First, break down what "no action" means. No request doesn't mean the scheduler hasn't received the task; having a request doesn't mean an action execution already exists. When on call, preserve the original request and current state before choosing the next branch. Don't create new records by rerunning.

```text
No action result
├─ No request object
│  └─ Go back to the request body; check ref, spec, parameters; stop if anything is missing
├─ Request exists, no task execution record
│  └─ Check the save path; don't manually add an action
├─ Task execution record exists, no action result
│  └─ Check requested, the scheduling entry, and the scheduled start time
├─ Already started running
│  └─ Check running, then switch to the worker logs
└─ Already in a terminal state
   └─ Preserve the original record; don't resend to verify
```

During review, we added a clarification on a point that's easy to confuse. You can't infer `task_name` just from log headings; the task execution record itself stores the task name. `route` is the branch position carried by the next task request and should not be used in place of an action reference. The record's `task_route` also cannot be reconstructed from branch numbers in old logs; early notes said "a negative number might indicate the default branch," but that statement has not been confirmed on review and is being retained among the old conclusions.

Per-item tasks changed the assessment in the first draft. The initial assumption was that as long as a task existed, it would proceed to a normal action request. The samples do not support that inference: the task had a per-item flag but no corresponding action execution. Further checks narrowed the difference down to the number of items. When `itemized` is true, it's not enough to establish that the overall task exists; `item_id` and `items_count` must also be examined in the same record. One sample with `items_count` equal to zero completed directly, without going on to create an action execution; only nonzero samples continued into the action request path.

This counterexample also limits the interpretation of policy delay. Delay incidents fall into at least three categories: no request was recorded at all, a request was recorded but has not run yet, and the scheduled start time has been pushed back. Calling all three a slow worker won't help locate the issue. If the record is already in a terminal state, stop rerunning and preserve the original values; if the record is not in a terminal state and the scheduled time has not changed, note the action reference, task name, and status, and hand off to scheduling for further confirmation.

The old procedure still reads, "Get the policy value first, then compare it against the scheduled start time." It does not specify which layer calculates the time, nor confirm whether retries can change the order in which the logs appear. Log ordering cannot fill that gap.

### Earlier assessment retained

> delay only affects task pickup by the worker, not the request record.

This was a working rule from the early investigation. The per-item samples have already made it unsuitable as a default assumption, but it was not removed in this revision. Why the empty-item case completes directly, and exactly which layer changes the scheduled time, still need further checking.

# Task Request and Policy Delay Troubleshooting Tree

When troubleshooting this type of incident, branch first by symptom rather than inferring ownership from the filename. The earliest records described everything as the task not running; only later did they separate request objects, task execution records, action execution, and policy delay. This page is still reached from the old entry point via `st2common/st2common/services/workflows.py`, so it retains several sections that are no longer suitable to follow directly.

## 2023-03-20: Trace Back from Log Names

The initial draft searched only along `workflow`, `state`, `task`, and `request`. The file-header dependencies that could be seen directly were:

```python
from __future__ import absolute_import
import copy
import retrying
from orquesta import conducting
```

The rule of thumb at the time was: if a request had action `ref`, and also had `spec`, first assume that a later worker would take over; `parameters` was treated as an ordinary action parameter, and no further effort was made to trace whether it affected the recovery path. When the logs left only a task name, the corresponding task was guessed from the name. This could locate the entry point for ordinary samples, but it did not distinguish task save records from action requests.

The initial sketch had only two lines:

```text
workflow
  |
  +-- request -- ref/spec/parameters --> action
  |
  +-- state --------------------------> scheduler
```

If a request log appeared but no execution log did, first trace back the request; if the request could not be found either, temporarily classify it as an omitted send by the caller. This determination did not distinguish between action execution having already been created but not yet run and the task execution record never having been saved. It only represented the method used at the time.

The initial draft also ended with an unresolved question: did policy delay change the scheduled start time when the request was created, or did it take effect only when the worker claimed the task? At that time there were no comparable time samples, so neither hypothesis was written as a conclusion.

## The First Stop Rule Added Next to the On-Call Page

Records that were still waiting had once been rerun directly. After the rerun, no comparable incident state was available, and the original scheduled time was also difficult to determine, so the on-call page later added a sentence: after seeing the request, first read the current status and scheduled start time; do not rerun before the terminal state has been confirmed.

```text
Found a task with no action result
├─ No task execution
│  └─ Stop: go back to the request body, check ref, spec, parameters
├─ task execution exists, status unchanged
│  └─ Check requested; do not treat waiting as running
├─ Already running
│  └─ Check action execution and worker logs
└─ Already in a terminal state
   └─ Stop: preserve the original record, no need to resend for verification
```

The `requested` and `running` here were initially just markers used during on-call shifts to distinguish waiting from running, and had not yet been matched individually against metrics or queue changes.`task_name` also still came from log excerpts that could easily become outdated, so the request object cannot be changed based solely on log titles.

This stop rule has a very specific purpose: it preserves the original time values from the delay incident. If it later turns out that the request body was missing fields, the task had not been saved or the worker had already taken over, we can still return to the same record to assess the situation, rather than face mixed results after a manual rerun.

## 2024-03-26: Per-item samples refute the claim that an action is always issued

During the per-item action review, we initially assumed that each item would go through one normal action request. The sample did not support this inference: the record showed that the task carried a per-item marker, but there was no corresponding action execution. We looked further down, and only then discovered that the sample had no pending items.

The procedure used in the incident was therefore changed to two steps: first check the per-item marker, then check the item count. When the count is zero, accept the task as complete and do not send an additional action request; when the count is greater than zero, then check each item's concurrency window and whether a request was actually generated. It was still unclear at the time where delay was calculated, and the old record only said "the worker may pick it up after a delay".

Another failure path came from task routing. Someone rebuilt the task using the branch number from the logs, and the resulting object did not match the task in the record. Two names were provisionally retained after review:`route` is used for the branch position of the next task carried in the request, while `task_route` remains in the task execution record. The old draft did not specify numeric constraints, so negative numbers cannot be interpreted as the default route.

This review left us with a narrower conclusion: the existence of the overall task does not mean that a request has already been made for every item. In per-item scenarios, check the task itself first, then the items; do not infer whether the task was created successfully from the action count.

## 2024-03-27: Review margin notes

Two short notes were left after the review, preserved verbatim:

> First establish whether a task execution record exists, then discuss why the action did not run. Empty per-item tasks cannot be explained using the path for a regular action.

> For policy delay, distinguish between three scenarios: no request, a request that exists but has not run, and a scheduled time that has been pushed back.

The tree saved after the review is below. It is still a troubleshooting tree for actual incidents, not a comprehensive table of all workflow states.

```text
A. The request object is missing
   └─ Check the input fields; stop if ref, actions, or spec is missing
B. The request exists, but no task execution record exists
   └─ Check the saved task contents and creation delegation; do not manually add an action
C. A record exists, but the action has not run yet
   └─ Check requested, scheduler entries, and the scheduled start time
D. Already running
   └─ Check the worker and state transitions, do not rerun here
E. The per-item task has no items
   └─ Take the completion branch, do not create an action execution
F. The per-item task has items
   └─ Check each item's identifier and concurrency window
```

This review did not resolve the time reference for policy delay, nor did it address the notification task list. Both issues remain on the page, but they cannot be used to explain all waiting actions. In particular, the fact that a request already exists must still first be distinguished from whether a task execution record exists.

## Retained but deprecated manual time-adjustment method

The old operational guidance once read: first change the scheduled time back to the current time, then observe whether the worker picks it up. This approach destroys the original timing evidence and was later marked as deprecated, but the original text was not deleted. When the scheduled time is abnormal, first save the original values of the request object, task state, and scheduling queue; if policy delay still cannot be distinguished from a queue-read issue, stop at this layer.

There was another misreading at the same stage: action references are only useful when creating requests. A later recheck changed the order. The action definition must also be retrieved again when restoring a task, otherwise the runner and parameter information may not be on the same path. This correction only changed the recheck order, it did not rewrite old requests into the new format.

Another statement no longer in use is "As long as there is a task, an action will be sent". Empty per-item tasks are a counterexample. This sentence was not removed from the old page because some old on-call excerpts are still organized around it; when handling an actual incident, check the number of items first, then determine whether an action is missing.

## 2025-08-28: Revised wording before release

Initially, delay was attributed to the worker being slow to pick it up, but that wording can no longer be used. A missing request, a task record that was not saved, a request that has been retained but has not yet run, and a scheduled start time that has been pushed back are four different incident scenarios. They can appear together in nearby log entries, but the same remedial action should not be used for all of them.

From this point on, investigation records no longer require you to infer the object from the log title. First save the original request, task execution record, current state, and scheduler entry; if the record is already in a terminal state, stop rerunning it. If the record is not yet in a terminal state and the scheduled time has not changed, retain the action reference, task name, state, and original time value, and continue checking the scheduling path. Only if the scheduled time has been pushed back should policy delay be treated as the main branch.

This change in wording has not turned the old page into a unified explanation of states. It merely separates the waiting conditions that were previously conflated and removes manual time changes from the default actions. The tree below remains a valid starting point for an investigation.

## Follow the tree by symptom

```text
Task did not start as expected
├─ 1. Request body is missing
│  ├─ Are ref, actions, and spec present?
│  │  ├─ No -> Stop at the original request, preserve the input
│  │  └─ Yes -> Check the task execution record
│  └─ Record exists -> Go to 2
├─ 2. Task execution record exists but has no action
│  ├─ Is itemized true?
│  │  ├─ Yes -> Check items_count
│  │  │  ├─ 0 -> Direct completion is allowed, stop, do not request an action
│  │  │  └─ Greater than 0 -> Check item_id and the concurrency window for each item
│  │  └─ No -> Check whether request_action_execution was reached
│  └─ No evidence that creation was delegated -> Stop, do not guess the worker
├─ 3. action has been requested but has not run
│  ├─ Is the state requested?
│  │  ├─ Yes -> Check the scheduler entry and scheduled start time
│  │  └─ No -> First confirm whether the record reflects the latest state
│  └─ Already running -> Switch to the worker side, do not rerun from this page
└─ 4. policy delay looks wrong
   ├─ Scheduled start time has not been pushed back -> Check policy reads and scheduler logs
   ├─ Already pushed back -> Compare the saved value with the time observed during the investigation
   └─ Already in a terminal state or not runnable -> Save the queue value before cleanup, then stop
```

The first branch only handles request contents; the second branch only checks whether the task execution record and action creation are connected; only the third branch handles records that have been requested but have not yet run. Only upon entering the fourth branch does the scheduled start time become the main focus of policy delay. Do not infer that the time has already been calculated just because one log line appeared first, and do not overwrite the original record with the result of a rerun.

When an itemized task has no actions, read `itemized` and `items_count` first. When the count is zero, accept direct completion; do not manually create an action execution just to make the logs look complete. When the count is nonzero, `item_id` is used to determine whether a particular iteration item is still within the concurrency window where applying delay is allowed. This determination applies to the item and does not replace the status check for the task as a whole.

Do not conflate task names and routing either. `task_name` points to the task name in the workflow; `route` is the branch location carried by the next task request; `task_route` remains in the task execution record. The fact that all three appear near the same section of the logs does not mean they can substitute for one another.

## Current verification of the request surface

This section was added after old records, on-call supplements, itemized counterexamples, and deprecated operations, and is only for verifying the current request surface:

> Task requests preserve ref, actions, spec, route, task_name, task_route, itemized, item_id, items_count, request_action_execution, parameters, requested, and running; tasks lists are retained for notification and rerun. On public surface trigger lookup, dictionary dispatch checks id, then uid, then type with parameters.

Do not apply the fields used for trigger lookup back to ordinary task requests. At the public entry point, the dictionary first checks `id`, then looks up the stable identity by `uid`, or looks up the trigger type and parameters using `type` and `parameters`. This is the dispatch order for trigger lookup, not an alternative way to write task routing.

Inquiry validation should also not be inferred from ordinary task requests. This path uses the runner's `name` to confirm that the execution instance uses an inquirer runner. Its meaning differs from `task_name`: the former identifies the runner, while the latter stores the task name in the workflow.

Notifications and reruns share the name `tasks`, but do not merge the two paths because of that. Notifications can use a task list to identify the tasks that need to receive or apply notifications; reruns also pass a task list. Override values for reruns are placed in `parameters`, and must not be used to retroactively compensate for missing fields in task creation requests.

## Two issues not yet split out

After notifications are persisted, if the task list and configuration contents are inconsistent during recovery, there is no conclusion here on whether this should be recorded by workflow or interpreted on the notification side. The existing material is only sufficient to confirm that `tasks` will be retained, not to establish whether anomalous notifications will change action requests.

Another open issue is the relative order of scheduler logs and queue reads. The saved scheduled start time, current state, and queue entries are still more reliable than the order of log lines. If the two conflict, keep the original values and stop at the timing branch, without making manual corrections.

## Old appendix: The original simplified version

> 1. Find the task.
> 2. Check whether the request has a ref.
> 3. If you do not see an action, retry once.
> 4. The delay may just be due to a slow worker.

The first three steps were used only on the initial samples of regular tasks, and the fourth has been disproved by item-by-item samples and timing cross-checks. The appendix is retained because the old entry points may still lead troubleshooters here; for actual incidents, follow the symptom-based triage and stopping points above.

# History of Action Anomalies and Empty Items

This page was not originally an interface specification, but instead brought together two regression terms that could easily appear at the same time: malformed action references, and empty item completion for an itemized task. Both could appear during workflow creation or continued execution, but there was no evidence at the time that they belonged to the same failure point. Later reviews retained this juxtaposition, only separating the two paths in the record.

## Early Decisions on Paper

The early draft's judgment on malformed references was straightforward: if the action reference itself is not written in a parseable form, reject it during workflow validation; do not create an action execution first and then leave failure handling to action lookup or exceptions further downstream. The practical benefit was to preserve the original location within the task, while also allowing callers to distinguish "the reference is written incorrectly" from "the action has already run but failed" before creating an execution. Not all action errors were included at the time. Cases involving a parseable reference but a missing action definition, unsuitable parameters, or runtime exceptions occurring only after an execution had been created were still treated as separate troubleshooting paths.

Another option considered was to leave the check in lookup. To existing callers, this looked closer to the original entry point and might have changed exception timing less; the cost was that malformed references would surface later and might even get mixed in with some execution records. At the time, this cost was considered harder to manage than maintaining entry-point compatibility, so the notes favored upfront validation. However, the page did not retain any material showing whether existing callers depended on specific exception types or messages, so this compatibility impact cannot be described as an incident that actually occurred.

The decision for empty item completion was different. When the item count for an itemized task is already zero, the task completes directly, without sending a request with no business input to the action layer. Another idea was to create one execution through the normal task path so that the same kind of record would be visible afterward; this would make "no items" look like an actual action and make it difficult for existing troubleshooting procedures to distinguish empty input from an action failure. In the end, direct completion was retained, and no fabricated empty action was used.

These two decisions are not interchangeable. Samples with malformed references need to be checked for whether validation preserves the task location; samples with zero items need to be checked for whether action execution is skipped. Seeing only one branch pass is not enough to infer that the other branch has also been resolved.

## Entry Points and Boundaries

The old troubleshooting records linked the issue name and call name to `st2api/st2api/controllers/v1/actionexecutions.py`. This file is an existing Python module, with `import copy`, `import re`, `import sys`, and `import traceback` visible at the top. It can therefore serve as an entry point for tracing the code, and also explains why the old records placed reference validation, error returns, and action execution along the same code-reading path; these import statements alone do not prove that the two behaviors are performed by the same function.

When tracing the code, first look at the task location reported by workflow validation, then check whether action lookup has already occurred. If an error appears only during definition parsing or parameter validation, it should not be retroactively recorded as a malformed action reference. If an action execution has already been created, subsequent runtime exceptions must not be relabeled as pre-creation validation failures either. This boundary reflects how later reviews narrowed the early draft's use of "downstream exceptions": the early draft's scope was too broad, making it easy to conflate three different points in time.

The check for empty items starts with the task's item count. If the count is zero, state transitions should stop at the task-completion path; only if the count is nonzero should processing continue down the normal action-request path. What is retained here is a historical decision, not a complete description of the entire workflow lifecycle. The original record did not provide the name of the responsible workflow or a specific entry point for rollback.

## Trade-offs Recorded During Review

Upfront rejection changes when a failure occurs. If existing callers only care whether something fails, the change may be small; if they inspect the old exception types or messages, the change needs to be checked separately. The current material contains no caller code, so this is recorded only as a compatibility cost, without adding a compatibility table that does not exist. Although rejection within lookup is closer to the old path, it sacrifices clarity about the task location and may also leave some records behind before failing.

Direct completion also has a visible cost: callers that rely on action execution records to observe tasks will not see an execution representing empty items. This cost has been deliberately retained, because creating an execution with no input would change the meaning of "task completion". The page provides no evidence that all observers have adapted, so it does not present this as unconditionally compatible.

````text
Simplified notes from the early draft:
Malformed reference -> check first; zero items -> complete directly
````

The old sentence above is still useful, but should not be used on its own to prove where the behavior is implemented. It only preserves the direction of the decision at the time. Formal tracing still starts at the file entry point, with separate notes on the input format, the timing of lookup, and whether an execution was created.

## Records Added Later

ST2-206 later moved first into `release_classified`, then transitioned to `work_started`. The check added by the card was: confirm whether the handling of malformed action references is in effect in a real CI run, and do not treat the existence of a configuration file as a run result. This page has not filled in a nonexistent job URL, nor has it rewritten the check as "passed".

ST2-223 included samples related to empty item completion and requested tracing the build logs to find the actual execution steps, then filling in the responsible workflow and rollback entry point. The samples show that there is material to continue tracing, not that this page already knows the specific workflow. Thus, "complete directly when there are zero items" remains the retained decision, while the responsible entity and rollback location remain blank.

These two additions did not overturn the early draft. They shifted the page away from the old impression that "the two terms might refer to one problem" and toward two adjacent branches: one decides whether to reject during input reference validation, and the other decides whether to skip action execution when the item count is zero. Both can be followed starting from the same file, but the same output cannot serve as interchangeable evidence for the two.

## Old Options That Were Not Removed

"Let errors be raised downstream first, then handle them together" was not deleted, because it explains why early troubleshooting started at the action execution entry point. "Create one execution even for zero items, to make observation easier" is also retained among the historical trade-offs; it was an option evaluated for comparison, not a current practice that this page is seeking to restore. There is no readily available record of whether existing callers still rely on these two observation methods.

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> WorkflowCheck
    WorkflowCheck --> MalformedRejected: malformed action reference
    WorkflowCheck --> ActionLookup: reference accepted
    WorkflowCheck --> ItemCountCheck: itemized task
    ItemCountCheck --> Completed: zero items
    ItemCountCheck --> ExecutionRequested: items present
    ActionLookup --> ExecutionRequested: normal path
    MalformedRejected --> [*]
    Completed --> [*]
    ExecutionRequested --> [*]
```

Currently, only two specific gaps remain on this page:

- [ ] Confirm the failure location and regression results for malformed action references in a real CI run;
- [ ] Locate the workflow associated with empty item completion from the build logs for ST2-223, and record the rollback entry point.

ST2-206, ST2-223 are for navigation only. The entry point for tracing the code is still `st2api/st2api/controllers/v1/actionexecutions.py`; this page does not have enough material to extend that entry point into a complete call chain.

# History of Malformed Actions and Empty Items: Current Scope Decision

Use the pinned offline environment and isolated backend substitutes for local development while exercising the real production entry points.
