# Action Output and Completion Lock Migration

This page originally grouped action result display, output validation, and completion serialization into a single migration track. That approach was convenient: the status returned by a command was treated as a signal both that the result had been confirmed and that completion had been handled. The old record has not been deleted because it explains why recovery actions always started on the command side.

However, the old framing also skewed the scope of troubleshooting. Whenever an issue description contained action, someone would open `st2client/st2client/commands/action.py` and treat it as the place to change all related behavior. That path is indeed an entry point reachable from the old troubleshooting records through issue names and call names, and the file does contain contiguous display logic; but this is not enough to classify serialized completion handling as command formatting.

## The Previously Recorded Migration Rationale

The old version's core assumption was: first make the action result "look right", then use that same result to determine completion; whenever the two diverged, roll back to command output. It treated the caller-facing display and completion handling as a single recovery surface, assuming this would both preserve the display and restore serial processing.

This assumption is no longer used as an operational basis. It did not distinguish between "the result seen by the caller" and "the completion order has been checked", nor did it explain where the lock state should be stored. The old page reduced this gap to a single stopping condition: continue as long as the result is normal. This stopping condition reflects only the migration practices at the time; it does not mean that the completion side was independently confirmed.

The old manual also assumed that all anomalies could be rolled back from the same place. Parameter display, workflow instance display, status summaries, individual execution status, and completion order are actually different troubleshooting targets. Rolling them all back at once may quickly return to the old path, but it obscures which change actually affected the caller.

The sequence diagram used at the time is retained below. The arrows indicate only the troubleshooting direction in the old record, not module calls.

```text
Action request
   |
   v
Result display ─────────> Treated as complete
   |                    |
   +----Roll back on anomalies-------+
```

The most problematic part of this diagram is the judgment on the right. Result display is the end visible on the command side; "treated as complete" is a separate judgment. The former can change because of changes in parameter or status formatting, while the latter still needs its own job records. The old diagram connected the two with a single arrow, making it easy to roll back unrelated display changes during recovery.

## Entry Points Still Available on the Command Side

`st2client/st2client/commands/action.py` is worth retaining as a reference point for reviewing old output. The following neighboring functions can be located in this file:

- `format_parameters(value)`;
- `format_wf_instances(instances)`;
- `format_execution_statuses(instances)`;
- `format_execution_status(instance)`.

They handle the display of parameters, workflow instances, instance status summaries, and individual instance status, respectively. To preserve the form seen by legacy callers before migration, retain comparisons for these four categories of objects rather than capturing only the final line of command output. Even when parameters, instance lists, and status text belong to the same command output, they may be formatted in different places.

The comparisons here serve only compatibility checks for action output validation. For example, more consistent parameter formatting may make the result look as though the new path has taken effect; this only shows that the output layer has changed. If the ordering of workflow instances or the status text remains unchanged, that too only shows that the corresponding display objects can still be explained. These observations do not establish that completion has proceeded serially as expected.

Similarly, if status output changes, do not immediately call it a lock issue. First distinguish between summary status and individual status. For the summary object, refer back to `format_execution_statuses(instances)`; for the individual object, refer back to `format_execution_status(instance)`. If neither shows any display differences, the command-side records have no grounds for drawing conclusions about the completion side.

The file also contains `ActionBranch`, its `__init__`, and `ActionListCommand`. The old version listed these names under the "completion path", mainly because they were all in the same action command file. This association has been abandoned: proximity in names and line numbers can only help reopen the same section of command-side code; it does not show that these objects control serialized completion. This correction is retained to prevent adjacent objects in the file from being mistaken for an execution chain during the next investigation.

Likewise, `os`, `ast`, and `copy` at the top of the file only indicate that the module has these direct dependencies. They do not fill in the missing location of the lock implementation, nor do they constitute evidence that output validation and completion handling share code. The old record failed to make this distinction, turning "you can start looking here" into "you should make the change here".

## The First Batch Migrating Away from Old Output

The first batch handles only the callerFang Ke-visible portion of action output validation. Before starting, preserve how parameters, workflow instances, summary status, and individual status appear in the old output; after the change, check the same objects one by one. There is no need to replace all four types of objects at once. If an item has not changed, retain its existing display; if an item causes a compatibility issue, restore only the corresponding formatting path.

If the parameter object behaves abnormally, return to the old display associated with `format_parameters(value)`. If the instance list behaves abnormally, return to `format_wf_instances(instances)`. Handle summary status and individual status separately as well; do not revert the other three just because one is abnormal. The old manual used a full rollback, which broadened the troubleshooting scope; this revision retains the old recovery entry points but no longer recommends rolling back the entire command output together.

The stopping point for this batch should also remain narrowly defined: if the command-side differences still cannot be explained by one of the categories of parameters, instances, status summaries, or individual status, stop the output compatibility attempt for now. Do not attribute unexplained differences to completion serialization simply to make the record look complete. This is exactly how the old version tied the two objects back together.

ST2-209 is the navigation entry point for action output validation. The card description calls for checking the relevant configuration closure and going to the corresponding repository file for each missing item. Later records include one reproduction action for this card, but neither a list of configuration items nor specific modification results is saved here. It can therefore direct people to where they can continue checking, but it cannot replace local output comparisons or be presented as proof of completion handling.

## Completion Serialization as a Separate Batch

Only the second batch inventories the current dependencies for serialized completion. It should not start automatically from "the result has been displayed", but should be logged separately after the display objects in the first batch can be explained. The identified direction for this batch is to trigger the corresponding job through the existing automation entry point and record the job, commit, and actual artifact name. ST2-226 retains this direction, but does not record job results, lock state, wait time, or implementation files on this page.

Therefore, the second batch's records must not fabricate a passing condition. If the job has not left enough job, commit, and artifact information, stop short of confirming the completion path. At this point, the available action is to restore the original completion path, not to change the display of parameters, instances, or execution status instead to create the illusion of "normal results".

The relationship between the two batches can be handled as shown below. Here, "acceptable" means only that the command-side display can be explained by the same set of formatting objects; it does not mean that the completion lock has been verified.

```text
Old output
  |
  +-- Parameter / instance / status display checks --Mismatch--> Restore old output
  |
  +-- Display acceptable -----------------------> Record completion job
                                             |
                                             +-- Unconfirmed --> Restore old completion path
```

This diagram has one more stopping point than the old diagram. When the first batch fails, it is the output compatibility attempt that is rolled back; the completion path is not canceled along with it. When the second batch remains unconfirmed, retain the display comparisons already completed in the first batch and restore the previous completion handling separately. Each type of rollback leaves different evidence, so the next check does not need to guess again whether the problem lies in parameters, instances, status, or the completion job.

The old page described "output passed" as permission to enter completion handling. It can now be treated only as the condition for ending the first batch: the command-side display has no unexplained compatibility issues. It is neither the lock state nor an artifact of an automation job. This correction has not removed the old paragraphs, because some legacy callers still make judgments based on result text, and looking back at the old framing explains their recovery order.

## What to Retain When Restoring the Old Path

When a client compatibility issue arises, first determine whether it belongs to parameters, the instance list, summary status, or individual status. Restore only the old display at the corresponding formatting entry point, and retain the current comparisons for the other objects. This avoids reverting workflow instances and status text together because of a single display issue, only to be unable to determine afterward which item actually affected the caller.

While the completion-side job has not yet left any records, do not delete the command-side samples. After restoring the old completion path, the comparisons of parameters, instances, and status can still serve as the starting point for the next output check. Conversely, after restoring command-side output, do not describe "successful recovery" as serialized completion having been restored; the evidence for these two recovery actions is not the same.

The old record's instruction to "remove the newly added completion checks and retain only action result formatting" still explains the early operations, but it is too coarse-grained. It bound output changes and completion changes into a single rollback, making it impossible either to preserve displays that had stabilized or to track unconfirmed jobs separately. If the old path must be used going forward, handle it in the two batches described on this page; do not copy that old stopping condition.

## Items Not Yet Added

- The job, commit, and actual artifact name for the job referenced by ST2-226 have not yet been recorded on this page.
- The configuration closure mentioned in ST2-209 still needs to be traced item by item to repository files through the card entry point.
- Whether the command-side adjacency of `ActionBranch` and `ActionListCommand` affects legacy callers has not yet been verified.
- DOC-20 documents another set of validation designs; this page does not carry those conclusions over into the action result compatibility migration.

This record retains the old judgments and recovery methods, but no longer treats command results as a substitute record for completed.

# Scheduler Logging Return Shape Decision

The earliest record left behind contained two work names side by side: scheduler logging, public return shape. They appeared in the same round of Quality and Regression review, so they entered the same long-term record; but being recorded together does not mean the implementation, ownership, or compatibility surface are also together. The decision after review remains to verify them separately, with the questions each line must answer made more specific.

The initial draft was not about the choice of "whether to do logging," but about where to begin making changes. The earlier investigation traced the issue name and the call name `get_logging_config_path` to `st2actions/st2actions/notifier/config.py`. If this file were directly treated as the shared implementation location for both requirements, configuration changes and public-result changes would happen simultaneously, making it difficult during regression to determine whether the path, configuration object, or result received by the caller had changed. Conversely, if they were completely split into two unrelated records, the context that they were found together in the same review round would be lost. In the end, the association is retained, but the change entry points are not merged.

## The Initial Draft's Choice

Three approaches were actually compared at the time:

| Option | Approach at the time | Problem left behind |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Merge handling | Handle logging configuration and the return result together near the configuration file | Two externally visible surfaces change together, making exceptions difficult to classify |
| Separate confirmation | Track them in the same group while separately locating the configuration entry point and return boundary | Two verification tracks must be maintained; one filename cannot stand in for the other piece of evidence |
| Record only the issue names | Retain only the two names, scheduler logging and public return shape | It would later be impossible to distinguish configuration delivery, result wrapping, and caller reads |

The decision was to adopt "separate confirmation." Here, "separate" is an arrangement of change order and evidence responsibility, not a claim that the two can never have a shared adaptation layer. Only when reference relationships show that they actually pass through the same adaptation point should the cost of merging the changes be compared again. This preserves their connection to the same-round regression while avoiding premature interface conclusions based on file location.

## Look at the Configuration Side First

The frozen entry point is:

`internal/st2-control` / `v_prev`  
`st2actions/st2actions/notifier/config.py`

The direct adjacency relationship left in the file header is:

```python
from __future__ import absolute_import
from oslo_config import cfg
import st2common.config as common_config
from st2common.constants.system import VERSION_STRING
```

`cfg` and `common_config` make this a reasonable starting point near the configuration object; `VERSION_STRING` indicates that the file also touches system version constants. This local relationship is sufficient to support the decision to begin verification from the configuration side, but insufficient to support broader conclusions such as "the scheduler's runtime logic is here" or "the public return wrapper is also handled here."

The items to verify on the logging side have been narrowed to three. First, exactly where the configuration path is declared or computed. Second, whether the caller receives a path, a configuration result, or something passed through another adaptation. Third, what result is actually left when configuration retrieval fails. The earlier investigation included `conf/logging.scheduler.conf`, so this exact string must be retained during the recheck to confirm whether it really is the externally exposed logging configuration path; until the declaration and call chain line up, it must not be written up as a settled interface based on its name alone.

This is also where `get_logging_config_path` fits. It can serve as a navigation clue to reconnect the old scheduler logging record to the configuration entry point; it is not itself a reference relationship and cannot alone prove the caller, return object, or failure handling. If the actual references lead the final entry point elsewhere, the decision should follow the references rather than insist on the directory location.

## How to Draw the Boundary on the Return Side

public return shape must be traced back from the actual location where it is delivered to the caller. The question is not whether an internal function has temporarily put a field somewhere, but whether the call boundary ultimately delivers a normal return value, a wrapper object, or an exception. Fields owned by an internal configuration object do not automatically become public fields; fields added by the wrapper layer cannot be inferred backward as native content of the configuration file.

One compatibility risk is retained here. If a default wrapper is added directly on the configuration side, a configuration-loading failure that was previously visible may become a different result, and callers may also begin to depend on fields that have not yet been confirmed. Conversely, if the internal configuration object is handed directly to the caller, its internal layout will be brought into the public interface, constraining future changes. Both approaches change the return boundary, so this version has not approved default fields, fallback objects, or a fixed return structure without reference verification.

The only decision that can currently be made on the return side is the verification method: first find the actual call boundary, then record the objects or exceptions before and after the boundary; do not use the existence of `config.py` to fill in a field list. No frozen material identifies a specific caller, public fields, or exception branches, so these items remain unconfirmed rather than being filled in with local evidence from the logging configuration.

## Responsibility Split After Review

On the configuration side, this path bears the "entry point" responsibility: start with the file declaration, direct dependencies, and old call name, and continue verifying the actual references. It is not the automatic owner of all scheduler logging behavior. Log text, log levels, and deployment differences are also outside this decision because the current material provides no implementation evidence for these behaviors.

The return side is assigned to the implementation location that owns the public call boundary. Once the configuration-side review is complete, it can at most explain how the configuration result is formed and delivered; it cannot decide the wrapping protocol for the return side. If the return-side review discovers a shared adaptation layer, only then is there reason to place the two tracks back into the same change assessment; until then, any change to "unify the return while we're at it" must be treated as an additional interface change.

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> grouped_review
    grouped_review --> logging_line: scheduler logging
    grouped_review --> return_shape_line: public return shape
    logging_line --> config_py_entry
    config_py_entry --> reference_check
    return_shape_line --> boundary_check
    reference_check --> separate_confirmation
    boundary_check --> separate_confirmation
    separate_confirmation --> [*]
```

The two verification branches in the diagram express a record relationship, not a new implementation conclusion: the logging line enters reference verification from the frozen file entry point, the return line enters shape verification from the call boundary, and they finally converge on the decision to confirm them separately.

## Decisions Currently Retained

1. scheduler logging and public return shape remain associated in the same round of quality rechecking, but are confirmed separately.

4. `conf/logging.scheduler.conf` is retained as the exact path that must be checked during the recheck; it must not be expanded into a complete logging protocol when the evidence is insufficient.
5. Before the public call boundary is found, do not write the configuration object, default fields, or exception wrapper as the established public return shape.
6. Only after a shared adaptation layer has been confirmed by the reference relationship should the compatibility costs of merged and separate changes be compared again.

This revision adds the scope of applicability of the decision, rather than predesigning a return protocol. The configuration side already has a specific file, direct dependencies, and a call name; the return side still must be confirmed by the actual delivery boundary. # Proposal for Runner Aliases and Cumulative Integration

The scope of this proposal has not changed: runner alias loading and the version differences it causes in cumulative integration. The starting point for verification is still `st2common/st2common/runners/utils.py`. First, note the adjacent entries visible in the file header: `from __future__ import absolute_import`, `import os`, `import logging as stdlib_logging`, `import six`. This is enough to locate the loading utility, but not enough on its own to establish the relationships among all callers.

The early draft framed the problem as "each caller changes the old name to the new name." On review, that conclusion was premature. If even two callers retain different conversion methods, cumulative integration results will vary by call path; and when loading fails, the name in a screenshot may not be the name for which plugin discovery failed. We first need to record the original input value, the names tried, and the configuration ultimately passed to the plugin separately.

### Interface behavior to preserve initially

The recommendation is to trial compatibility handling inside the loader rather than scatter conversion tables across callers. The tentative order is:

- Run the existing lookup with the original runner name first;
- Only try the agreed aliases if the original name is not found;
- After finding a plugin, still use the original caller's `config` mapping to call `get_runner`;
- If the original name succeeds, do not enter the alias branch or change the returned object.

This is only a candidate implementation; the alias rules have not been finalized. At a minimum, the rules must specify whether underscore, hyphen, and case variants of a name are interchangeable, and whether matching multiple plugins should produce an error immediately. Without these constraints, "compatibility" may just turn a clear lookup miss into an inconsistent false match.

### Two implementation locations

The advantage of putting this in the loader is that verification for cumulative integration only needs to happen in one place, and callers can still submit their original names. The trade-off is that the loader must handle alias precedence and conflict diagnostics, and legacy caller Fang Ke may not be able to see what they passed in.

The advantage of putting this in callers is that each call site can explicitly declare the post-migration name, and errors surface closer to the business entry point. The trade-off is that conversion tables will diverge as the number of callers grows; callers missed in the change will still use the old path, making it look as if one version has two kinds of runner behavior. For this work, try the loader-based approach first; modifying multiple callers at once is not an acceptable first step.

### Review references and trial boundaries

ST2-212 can be used to return to the original entry point for runner alias loading. At the review of the second version, what was missing was not another name but a failing sample from a caller, so the proposal could not be written up as a verified fix at that point. The sample still needs to be compared against the usable artifact from the previous round; ST2-229 are only pointers to version differences in cumulative integration, not a substitute for that sample.

The trial has three fixed input categories: success with the original name, a miss on the original name where an alias should match, and a name conflict. For each category, retain the contents of the supplied `config` and check that the compatibility logic has not rewritten the configuration the loader passes to `get_runner`. With only alias samples and no original-name samples, we cannot tell whether the old path has been broken; if we only have caller screenshots and not the actual input values, stop at the reproduction-preparation stage.

### Rollback and open items

Rollback is straightforward: remove the compatibility fallback and restore the single load attempt with the original name, without retaining a new caller-side conversion table. Rollback triggers include entering the alias branch even though the original name succeeds, silently choosing among conflicting matches, inconsistent `config` between the two paths, or different callers getting different plugins for the same alias.

The formal alias set, the error shape for conflicts, and which callers will write the migrated names into their configuration are still undecided. Decide these three points after obtaining a failing sample; until then, this page supports a single centralized trial, not a declaration that the alias loading interface is complete.

# Per-item task persistence troubleshooting tree

The per-item task results differ from the usable artifact from the previous round. Start by keeping the investigation scoped to "whether task persistence contributed to the difference." Don't start by changing the workflow definition, and don't assume the entire task has been reliably persisted just because one item has completed.

Whoever is on shift should first capture three sets of evidence: the name of the task that triggered the difference; the counts of completed and incomplete items in the same workflow; and whether rereading returns the record seen earlier or a different record. If any of the three is missing, don't expand the investigation to the scheduler or runner. The check here is whether the task object matches the item-level observations, not to guess which component is at fault.

```text
Results differ
├─ Did the task reach the persistence side?
│  ├─ No: go back to request creation and note the conditions under which it did not reach persistence
│  └─ Yes: read the record for the same task
├─ Can the reread record still be matched to the original task?
│  ├─ No: retain the object being read and its context, and stop retrying
│  └─ Yes: compare item counts and completion status
└─ Does the difference appear only after a restart or recovery?
   ├─ Yes: check the workflow persistence entry point
   └─ No: check against the normal task path first
```

Earlier investigation notes point to `st2common/st2common/persistence/workflow.py` as the entry point. When you open it, first examine the file's connections to `transport`, `db`, and `wf_db_models` separately. Don't write up model reads, data access, and subsequent handoff as a single operation. If you can't find the expected record at this step, don't clear old state to manufacture a clean result; preserve the original record and the read sequence.

This is only a working hypothesis: anomalies in per-item tasks aren't necessarily caused by a single item, and the task object reread during recovery may also change what you observe. Conditions for a reliable reproduction haven't been isolated yet.

# Per-item task persistence troubleshooting tree

When a per-item task and the previous usable artifact produce different results, first check whether the discrepancy has reached task persistence. Don't start by changing the workflow definition, and don't treat one item's completed result as proof that the entire task-level record is correct. The initial draft required recording the task name, the counts of completed and unfinished items, and whether a reread returned the old or new record. Keep all three, but the review found that the location of the read was also missing.

Break the investigation down into creation, writing, reading, and continued processing. For each stage, retain only the minimum object relationships, all from the same run. Matching task names aren't enough to establish that the evidence can be combined: objects obtained from different artifacts, different jobs, or different recovery stages must not be mixed into one sample.

```text
Results differ
├─ Can per-item processing be confirmed around the request?
│  ├─ No: record the relationship between the task and request; stop at the request side
│  └─ Yes: examine the objects after the write
├─ Can the task record be read again after the write?
│  ├─ No: retain the last visible object; do not retrigger the original run
│  └─ Yes: compare the task-level record with the item observations
├─ Do both sides come from the same run and the same read stage?
│  ├─ No: record them separately; they cannot be compared on this basis
│  └─ Yes: mark when the discrepancy appears in the sequence
└─ Does the discrepancy become visible only after recovery or continued processing?
   ├─ Yes: retain the two objects read before and after the action
   └─ No: return to the first readable object after the write
```

The review table no longer starts with "has the task finished." Fill it in by observation point instead:

| Observation point | What to retain | What not to infer at that point |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Before and after request creation | The mapping between this run's task and workflow | The task record has already been written |
| Around the write | A task object that can be reread | Every item follows the same path |
| Around continued processing | The order in which item results and task-level status appear | This read reflects the final state |
| Around recovery | The read entry point and the object obtained | Recovery necessarily causes the discrepancy |

If there is no sign of per-item processing around the request, the issue cannot yet be assigned to persistence. Record the relationship between the task, workflow, and request for this run, then stop. The outcome of this branch is "no object obtained from before entry into persistence," not "persistence was not involved." If a retry is needed, start a separate run as a comparison; do not clean up, overwrite, or backfill items in the original run.

The absence of an object that can be reread around the write also does not justify recording "no write occurred." There may be intermediate transformations or transfers that this evidence did not capture. You can start investigating from `st2common/st2common/persistence/workflow.py`: the file visibly imports `transport`, `db`, and `wf_db_models`. First look around the model objects, then distinguish the boundary of a single storage access from the point where the object is handed to the next processing stage. This file is a starting point for verification, not the only home for per-item tasks.

When the task-level record doesn't match the item observations, first lay out both sides: what the task-level record shows and what is observed on the item side; whether they come from the same run and the same read, or one comes from before continued processing and the other from after recovery. Don't just record "item counts don't match," because that doesn't say whether the comparison is between pending counts, completed counts, or counts obtained at different points in time.

An older note suggested clearing old task records first, then retriggering the task to see whether a complete object could be read. After review, that suggestion is retained as a counterexample. Cleanup changes the conditions under which objects are retained, and retriggering changes the request source; even a successful later read cannot explain why the old record differed from the current result. Keep the original run read-only while it can still be read. If a new sample is truly needed, use it only as a separate comparison.

ST2-213 provides a starting point for comparison: when comparing against the previous usable artifact, update only jobs or pinned versions that have actually changed. After walking through that card, the sequence was changed to first pin down the artifacts and their respective jobs on both sides, then read the task object on each side. If only one side can be read, stop at "record availability differs." Only once both sides have objects should you compare the task-to-item mapping.

The initial draft's hypothesis is retained: the task object reread during recovery may change what is observed. The available evidence supports treating this only as an avenue to investigate, not attributing the discrepancy to a particular field or part of the call path.

# Item-by-Item Task Persistence Troubleshooting Tree

This old record is usually dug up from ST2-213. The card focuses on the difference between current-version results and the last available artifact, and requires updating only jobs or pinned versions that actually changed; it does not preserve all relationships among per-item tasks across creation, writing, reading, and recovery. The practices layered on during several on-call shifts are retained below. The short tree above can still be used to contain the incident, but it is no longer the only sequence.

First, write out the comparison. If these fields are not filled in, do not try to fill in the evidence by rerunning a broad workflow:

| Item | Fill in on the spot |
| --- | --- |
| Last available artifact |  |
| Current artifact or pinned version |  |
| Job corresponding to each side |  |
| Task name |  |
| Number of completed and incomplete items |  |
| Task object obtained from the first read |  |
| Where the second read occurred |  |
| Action between the two reads |  |
| Whether a restart, recovery, or continuation was involved |  |

"First" and "second" in the table do not stand for old and new objects. They only indicate the order of observation. Someone once combined a read before recovery with a read from another run, then used "an old record was read" to explain the discrepancy; that record is insufficient to show whether the object actually changed.

## Initial draft retained: contain the discrepancy first

The earliest record only knew that the per-item task results differed; it could not confirm whether the difference was in a particular item, a particular write, or a later read. Therefore, the initial draft did not provide a root-cause path and only required looking separately at task-level records and item-level observations.

```text
Results differ
├─ Did the task actually enter the persistence layer?
│  ├─ No: go back to request creation and record the conditions under which it did not enter
│  └─ Yes: read the record for the same task
├─ After rereading, can it still be matched to the original task?
│  ├─ No: retain the read object and context; stop retrying
│  └─ Yes: compare the item count and completion status
└─ Does the discrepancy appear only after a restart or recovery?
   ├─ Yes: check the workflow persistence entry point
   └─ No: first verify against the normal task path
```

The scope of this tree is narrow: do not treat "a given item already has a result" and "the task record was saved as expected" as the same thing. The three pieces of information most often missing during early incident response are the task name that triggered the discrepancy, the counts of completed and incomplete items within the same workflow, and whether the reread showed the original object or a different object. If any one of the three is missing, the investigation should not be expanded to the scheduler or runner.

The initial draft's references to "old records" and "new records" were also too rough. An object that appears older does not mean it came from an earlier write; it may simply have been read earlier or come from another run. The requirement to record the objects from both reads still stands, but each one must be annotated as occurring after request creation, after the write, during continuation, or after recovery.

The working hypothesis left by the initial draft is: the anomaly in per-item tasks may not be caused by a single item, and the task object reread during recovery may also change the observed result. This statement has neither been confirmed nor removed. Subsequent review only establishes that it is worth checking; it must not be rewritten as a conclusion about the recovery mechanism.

## Old margin note beside the file entry

The old troubleshooting notes pointed to `st2common/st2common/persistence/workflow.py` as the entry point. This entry point is still suitable for identifying object adjacency starting from the persistence side: the file visibly imports `transport`, `db`, and `wf_db_models`. The effective way to read it at the time was to first record three types of observations separately:

- Around `wf_db_models`, record whether workflow-related objects are being constructed, read, or converted;
- Around `db`, record whether a data-access boundary is crossed;
- Around `transport`, record whether existing objects are merely being passed to the next stage of processing.

These are not three mandatory call chains, nor does this mean that all three locations can explain the differences. This only prevents model reading, data access, and object passing from being lumped together as "writing a workflow." Having workflow in the filename likewise does not mean that every issue with per-item tasks should be attributed to this file.

The old notes contained a premature leap: going directly from the issue name to the read location, seeing that a task object could be read, and concluding that writes were working normally. That judgment was later retracted. Readability only shows that this read returned a result; it does not show that the current object is the same as the object in the comparison run, nor that the items underwent the same updates. If all that can now be established is "an object was seen after reading," stop at that statement rather than extending it into an attribution of responsibility to model conversion or persistence writes.

## Four locations added after review

The actual review shifted troubleshooting from "whether the task has finished" to four locations: creation, writing, reading, and continued processing. Take only the smallest snippet at each location, and all four pieces of evidence must come from the same run. Matching task names are not enough; records of tasks with the same name from different artifacts, different jobs, or different recovery stages cannot be stitched into a single timeline.

| Observation location | Object relationships to capture | What cannot be asserted at this step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Before and after request creation | The mapping between the task and the workflow for this run | The task record has already been saved |
| Around the write | Whether the task object can be read again | Every item underwent the same updates |
| Around continued processing | The order in which item results and task-level status appear | The current read reflects the final state |
| Around restart or recovery | The read entry point and the object obtained | The differences must have been caused by recovery |

"The same run" needs to be recorded along with the artifact and job. The requirement to compare ST2-213 is itself intended to avoid updating an unchanged job or pinned version. Even if two snippets have the same task name and the same item count, they cannot serve as evidence of before-and-after changes to the task record if they come from different jobs. Conversely, capturing request, write, and read snippets within a single run, even if no difference is ultimately found, is more useful than a complete narrative stitched together from three runs.

### Branch: Something is already wrong near the request

If you cannot confirm near the request creation point that the task is being handled as a per-item task, do not proceed to the persistence files yet. Clearly document the relationship between the task, workflow, and the current request, then stop. The stopping point here should be recorded as "no pre-persistence object for per-item processing was obtained", not "persistence was not involved". The latter conclusion goes beyond the currently available material.

If someone requests an immediate retry, first ask whether the retry will overwrite the original run. If the original object is still readable, do not clean it up or add entries to it; a new run can serve as a comparison, but it must be recorded in a separate column from the original run. The completed count from the new run must not be added to the original run, even if the task names are identical.

If only the task name remains on the request side, with no mapping between the task and workflow, you should not use the task name to guess the object in the persistence model either. This gap should remain documented in the handoff. At this point, digging further into `workflow.py` would only mistake a starting point for verification for a source of facts.

### Branch: No Rereadable Object After Writing

If no rereadable object can be found near the write point, record the last point where the task and its relationship to the entries were both visible. Do not rewrite "cannot read it" as "nothing was written": there may still be uncaptured points between creation, conversion, access, and transfer. You can start investigating near the model in `st2common/st2common/persistence/workflow.py`, but the record must identify this as a starting point for verification, not an already confirmed point of responsibility.

This branch is the most likely to trigger the old procedure: first clear the old task records, then launch the task again, expecting the next read to be clean. This procedure is now explicitly retained as a counterexample. Cleanup changes the conditions under which the object is retained, and retriggering also changes the request source; even if a complete object is read afterward, it cannot explain why the original record differs from the current result.

If the original object can still be read, keep it read-only. If a new sample must be generated on site, start a separate comparison run and document the new run as a new observation, without filling in conclusions about writes that the original run did not record. If the original object is no longer readable, record only "the original object can no longer be read" and the last visible point; do not infer its state before deletion from this gap.

### Branch: Task Records Are Readable, but Entries Do Not Match

First break "do not match" down into the two sides: what the task-level record shows and what is visible on the entry side; establish whether both were obtained in the same read, or one was obtained before processing continued and the other after resumption. Simply writing "the entry counts are inconsistent" is not useful, because readers do not know whether the comparison is between pending counts, completed counts, or counts obtained at different times.

```text
Task and entries do not match
├─ Are both sides from the same run?
│  ├─ No: record them separately, they cannot be compared
│  └─ Yes: continue
├─ Were both sides obtained in the same read phase?
│  ├─ No: state the order, then see whether it can be reproduced
│  └─ Yes: continue
├─ Does the discrepancy appear only after resumption?
│  ├─ Yes: retain the two objects read before and after resumption
│  └─ No: return to the first readable object after writing
└─ Can you confirm that a particular update overwrote the original object?
   ├─ Yes: record the update location, stop speculating further
   └─ No: leave it unconfirmed
```

Do not "fill in" data in this branch. Manually adding an item, retriggering the original request, or deleting an old object will all change the conditions for the next read. Unless the operation itself is part of an independent control run, do not patch the object under analysis. If the task-level records and item-level observations come from the same run but different read stages, preserve their sequence first rather than rushing to judge which side is closer to the final state.

Sometimes the two sides only appear inconsistent: one is the number of completed items, while the other is the number of unfinished items in the same workflow. The current material does not require them to add up to any fixed value. The troubleshooting notes should clearly state which objects were observed and where the data was retrieved, without turning an unestablished relationship between counts into a rule.

### Branch: Changes become apparent only after a restart, recovery, or continued processing

The initial draft pointed this phenomenon directly toward the workflow persistence entry point. That order was later revised. Restart, recovery, and continued processing are points in time, not causal attributions. First preserve what happened between the two reads: the object seen in the earlier read, the object after the action, and whether the action belonged to the same run. Only once the material is complete is it worth continuing the investigation from `workflow.py` toward the model or adjacent handoff points.

If the objects obtained before and after recovery cannot be unambiguously matched, stop the current record here. Do not write "recovery read the wrong old object"; that was only the initial draft's working hypothesis. If the objects can be matched and the difference first appears after recovery, you must still distinguish between two things: whether recovery revealed the difference, or whether a step during recovery changed the object. The existing records cannot choose between the two, so the on-site notes should say "the difference was first observed after recovery".

Continued processing must also be marked separately. Like recovery, it may merely allow a preexisting difference to be read, or it may introduce a change between the two reads. As long as you cannot identify the last consistent read and the first inconsistent read, do not call continued processing the cause of the update.

## Order for comparing artifacts

After ST2-213 was walked through, the troubleshooting order changed from "read the current results first" to "first pin down both sides of the comparison". This change is retained here because the old order made it easy to put outputs from different jobs on the same line.

1. Specify the available artifact from the previous run and the current artifact, and write the job on each respective side;
2. Separately record the task-level objects and item-level observations on each side;
3. Mark whether the read occurred after creation, writing, continued processing, or recovery;
4. First compare the material at the same point on both sides, then compare the before-and-after changes within each side;
5. Only when the objects, artifacts, and points in time can all be aligned should you record "the difference may be near persistence".

If task records are available on only one side, stop at "record availability differs". This means the current comparison is not yet valid; it does not mean that the readable side is correct or that the unreadable side definitely had no writes. If both sides have records but their read points differ, preserve that difference first as well, rather than directly comparing their counts side by side.

The card later went through a caller walkthrough, and also entered an in-progress state. These actions did not change this page's narrow scope: this page only covers the sequence of observations around itemized task persistence, and is not meant to explain every workflow recovery issue.

## Archived old procedures and corrections

### Deprecated: Clear records before rerunning

The old instructions were to clear old records when they were found, then trigger the task, and finally check whether the complete object could be read. This once made a subsequent read appear cleaner, but wiped out the very object that most needed to be compared. This action is no longer used to recheck itemized task persistence discrepancies.

The alternative is to preserve the original run and start a separate comparison run. The comparison run only produces new observations; these cannot be retroactively applied to the original run, especially not to claim that its task and items were once consistent after the write. If the original run has already been overwritten, just record the post-overwrite stopping point in the handoff.

### Corrected: A file entry point does not establish where the fault lies

In the past, some people attributed the issue to the persistence implementation as soon as they saw `st2common/st2common/persistence/workflow.py`. That claim has been corrected. This file is an entry point that can actually be inspected, and can help distinguish the local adjacency relationships of `wf_db_models`, `db` and `transport`; but discrepancies in itemized tasks may already have arisen before it, or may only become apparent during continued processing after the read.

File inspection also has a stopping point: if the material only shows that different objects were seen after the read, do not write that model conversion caused the inconsistency. If you can identify the last consistent read and the first inconsistent read, then record the actions between them for later verification.

### Still unresolved: The explanation after recovery

"The task object reread during recovery may also change the observations" remains a working hypothesis, not a troubleshooting conclusion. It is retained because objects from before and after recovery were indeed mixed together during the early investigation; but the existing material has not isolated the specific changes within recovery. When pursuing this point further, first fill in the relationship between the objects from the two reads, then decide whether to inspect object conversion or transfer near the persistence entry point.

## On-call stopping conditions

If any of the following occurs, do not expand the scope any further:

- It cannot be proven that the item observations and task observations come from the same run;
- The current artifact and the available artifact from the previous run have not each been matched to the corresponding job;
- The original object can no longer be read because it has been cleaned up or overwritten;
- Only the read result is visible, and its position relative to the request, write, continued processing, or recovery cannot be determined;
- The original run must be triggered again to obtain a so-called clean result.

Stopping does not mean closing the issue. Simply record the existing objects, the locations of the gaps, and the actions already performed. For this topic, making the gaps explicit is usually more useful than prematurely attributing the discrepancy to the persistence side.

The handoff only needs to retain the following few lines, without restating the entire tree:

```text
Comparison: Previous run artifact / Current artifact
job:
Task:
Itemized observations:
First readable object:
Second readable object:
Actions between the two:
Current stopping point:
```

"Itemized observations" should contain facts, not judgments. For example "A task-level object exists, and the item side comes from another read phase" can be retained; "There is a persistence problem" should not be entered when the objects and their positions in time have not been aligned. We can now confirm only that the file contains declarations used to organize arguments, workflow instances, and execution state; we cannot treat a nearby command object directly as a state handler.

The following locations are visible in the file:

```python
def format_parameters(value):
def format_wf_instances(instances):
def format_execution_statuses(instances):
def format_execution_status(instance):
```

This file also contains the constructor for `ActionBranch`, along with `ActionListCommand`. They can be checked in the same review to confirm which code the list command runs through. The `os`, `ast`, and `copy` imports at the top of the file provide no additional workflow state information; the earlier practice of inferring where post-run belongs from these nearby symbols has been abandoned.

There were actually three approaches on the table at the time.

- Treat the anomaly as a list-display issue and investigate `format_execution_status` directly. This is the lowest-cost option, but it assumes up front that the state data being assembled is already correct.
- Treat the anomaly as a state transition issue in workflow post-run. This looks beyond the client-side symptoms, but could miss inconsistencies between the values before and after formatting.
- Keep observations at both layers: first obtain the instance and state from the same post-run run, then compare them with the action list display. This option makes no claim about which layer is wrong; it simply avoids choosing where to make changes before there is enough evidence.

The decision remains the third option. This is an investigation sequence, not a workflow model for long-term reuse. If the instance state matches the command-line display, the client file provides only presentation-side leads; only if they differ do we return to the input/output relationships of `format_wf_instances`, `format_execution_statuses`, and `format_execution_status`. `format_parameters` is in the same module, but there is no reason to use it to explain the state discrepancy.

Follow this sequence during review. The state names in the diagram are checkpoints for this observation process; they do not imply that the product has an internal state machine with the same names.

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    state "Unexpected state after post-run" as symptom
    state "Workflow instance and state" as instance
    state "Command-line status display" as display
    [*] --> symptom
    symptom --> instance: Check first
    instance --> display: Then compare
    display --> [*]
```

This sequence also explains why the first draft did not go straight to changing the formatter. With only list output, we cannot distinguish a display discrepancy from a state discrepancy already present after post-run; with only the instance and no display from the same entry point, we cannot determine whether command-line processing contributed to the symptom. Both observations must come from the same rerun to be comparable.

One issue remains open: whether the files from a rerun can be reliably matched to the workflow instances in the list. # Proposal to Adjust the Caller Integration Testing Path

In the integration test records for contrib-client-integration, `workflow context` and `StatsD` are still on the same processing path. Both appear alongside call samples, but their failure exit points differ. Aggregating the results together at the end loses the distinction between a sample stopping at context propagation and not proceeding on the metrics side; a single failure record therefore cannot directly indicate where to look back.

This proposal is to try just one limited split: callers continue to provide `workflow context` through the original entry point, without having to change their existing integration first; metrics collection goes through separate adaptation logic alongside that entry point. Both parts still correspond to the same call sample, but their outputs are retained separately. During investigation, we can then first check whether the context has entered integration testing, and then whether the metrics adapter accepted the sample, rather than working backward from a combined failure exit.

The split is not intended to change what callers submit or make metrics adaptation a new mandatory integration layer. It simply provides two processing points that can be compared separately during the trial. If the context has arrived but metrics have produced no result, the issue should not be attributed to the caller first; conversely, if the metrics side has a record but the context has not proceeded, a single aggregated result must not hide that difference.

Another path we considered was to keep a single path and add unified failure aggregation at the end. Its advantages are fewer entry points, no additional adaptation boundary, and no need for callers to deal with both the old entry point and the split entry point. We did not adopt this approach, not because a single path is necessarily wrong, but because it collapses two distinct failure exits into one record. During integration testing, what we most need to establish is which side the sample stopped on; unified aggregation can only tell us that processing did not complete, not which side it stopped on.

Keep the old entry point in place before starting the trial. Records from both segments after the split must be traceable to the same call sample; otherwise, the two outputs cannot be compared side by side. The conditions for a trial are not met if the split requires callers to fully migrate first, or if existing samples cannot produce records on both the context and metrics sides. We do not assume that "the split is live," nor do we fill in missing collection records with zeros.

The rollback point is also limited to this trial: if sample correspondence cannot be maintained, or the old entry point cannot be retained, stop the split and restore the old entry point. Rollback means that this integration test did not provide sufficient conditions for comparison, not that the old path has been proven suitable for all subsequent integrations. Whether the new metrics adaptation is also removed depends on whether it can still independently retain records useful for the call samples; this has not yet been decided.

Three questions remain open:

- Which callers are still using `itemized task`;
- Whether the old entry point and the split entry point can retain comparable records for the same batch of call samples;
- Whether rollback should only restore the old entry point or also remove the new metrics adaptation.

The materials are still at `docs/adj-contrib/proposals/unadopted-contrib-client-integration-approach.md`. That location retains the main text and attachments; what is captured here is the trade-off made at the time: try the split first, retain the old entry point, and clearly document the rollback conditions when comparison is not possible.

# Compatibility Catalog Dual-State Postmortem

This anomaly is recorded alongside the compatibility catalog's migration records: the same object was marked with different states on two checks, and the entry point showed a different current revision each time. The inventories retained on the release and runtime sides can both still be opened, but neither can substitute for the other. For callers that depend on this catalog, the problem is not different page colors, but not knowing which version of the object they should maintain compatibility with.

When the issue was first recorded, the discrepancy was provisionally attributed to entry-point refresh lag. That assessment was enough at the time to explain the combination of "the old record was still there and the recovery page was already visible," so repeated attempts to overwrite the original record stopped. Looking back, that was only a working assessment, not a confirmed cause; the original record contains no complete sequence connecting the two revisions to the same update.

| Point in time | Recorded observation | Action at the time |
| --- | --- | --- |
| First check | The current entry point did not match the old record | Kept the first record seen; did not rewrite the old entry with the new state |
| Follow-up check | The recovery page was accessible, and both versions still coexisted | Stopped retrying and waited for the complete release/runtime inventories |
| After recovery | The object could continue to be used | Why the two states appeared at the same time remained unconfirmed |

The impact was concentrated in three areas: the public contract, migration records, and caller compatibility. A caller with only the recovery page would think the old revision had never existed; a caller working only from the old record would miss the object that had already been restored. The catalog itself has its own schedule, maintainer, and exit criteria, but this export did not preserve any parameters that could confirm the exit action, so the actual state cannot be inferred from the filename or the last successful display.

The retained file is `docs/adj-st2tests/incidents/st2tests-compatibility-catalog-two-states-for-one-object.md`. Its value is in preserving the fact that the two versions appeared side by side, as well as the point at which retries stopped; it does not provide a new set of catalog state definitions. The original "entry-point refresh lag" explanation remains here as a record of why the issue was not escalated immediately at the time, but it should no longer be treated as a conclusion about the cause.

After the recovery page appeared, the object's availability was no longer a blocker; the chain of explanation was still missing. What is missing is not more screenshots of the states, but the full command used at the time and its parameters, the revision corresponding to each of the two records, and whether there had been an unrecorded switch between the release and runtime inventories.

Open item: recover the full command used between the first record and the recovery page. Results obtained with parameters supplied later should be listed separately; they must not be retroactively presented as the initial observations.

# Alternative path proposal for the compatibility directory

This path was not adopted, but it is retained in the compatibility directory because the objections at the time were not about naming or presentation preferences. They were about whether callers could distinguish the failure exits. The initial comparison was left at `inquiry` versus `Mongo state`: the former kept the existing entry point, while the latter separated status reads from directory checks. The two sections had different failure exits; if the same layer still handled both, callers would see similar outward results but have to trace back in different directions.

The preference at the time for separating out `Mongo state` did not mean it was already more reliable than the old entry point. After the split, the directory side would need to know when to hand off for a status read, and callers could no longer treat the two kinds of failure as the same problem. This extra wiring was a cost of the proposal. Another unresolved point was `coordinator lock`: without confirming which callers were in use, the lock scope could not be documented as an assumption that would remain valid after the split.

## Retained candidate approach

The candidate path was not meant to replace the default entry point for st2tests-compatibility-catalog, but to retain an alternative carrier alongside the original entry point for comparison. The post-review addendum listed `workflow context` as a candidate carrier, but it only served to hold directory information in the discussion; changing the context name was not grounds for inferring that the failure boundaries had been separated.

Keep the same directory input and the initial output for the comparison. The old entry point continues to use `inquiry` for processing; the candidate entry point then goes through `workflow context` to reach the separate status section. What matters is not whether a run finishes, but whether callers can identify the failure as coming from directory checks or `Mongo state`; if both sides still provide only the same attribution, the split has not delivered enough benefit to offset the integration cost.

The review addendum required adding opposite-case inputs, so the validation window remained open. These inputs should exercise each of the two exits once: a sample that exercises only one exit is not enough to compare the paths. Without this set of opposite-case inputs, a partial green result should not be used as grounds for adoption, nor should the scope be expanded to more directory callers.

## Why it was not adopted

One objection to the split was straightforward: the maintenance surface would change from one entry point to two sections. Directory issues would require checking `inquiry`, while status issues would require checking `Mongo state`; a small change might touch both locations. One point in favor of retaining the candidate path was also narrow: if callers could directly distinguish the two failure exits with the same input, tracing back would involve one less guess. Neither side treated "clearer" as a proven conclusion.

The candidate path's withdrawal conditions are therefore not written as a release commitment. In any of the following cases, stop at the comparison stage: the opposite-case inputs cannot distinguish the exits; the call boundary for `coordinator lock` is still unconfirmed; the candidate entry point looks different only if its display labels are changed; or, after restoring the old entry point, the directory checks can no longer be verified in the original way. On withdrawal, return to the old entry point first; whether the state left by the candidate wiring needs separate handling still depends on how it is written, and that handling is not assumed to be complete.

## Where to find follow-up records

ST2B-003 contains records of the borrowing and return windows for the current revision, along with later document rechecks and work-start activity; it is useful for looking back at the state of the resources the comparison depended on at the time. ST2B-004 documents rerunning the current entry point after a cold start, explicitly without touching the shared cache. ST2B-008 requires rerunning the proposal that was not adopted in another environment, which can address whether the failure seen in one environment is reproducible. ST2B-013 requires exporting the maintenance entry point and exit actions before switching environments; after the environment changes, the results are no longer described as part of the same comparison round.

ST2B-009 provides version-sync clues: the baseline was retained first, followed by a handoff to the current module maintainer because the existing implementation had been reviewed. This change shows that the maintenance entry point was adjusted, not that callers have validated the candidate path. The related records are only references for tracing back; this proposal still records only the path that was not adopted, the objections, and where to stop when withdrawing it.

The maintenance file is `docs/adj-st2tests/proposals/unadopted-st2tests-compatibility-catalog-approach.md`. Two items remain open: the callers currently using `coordinator lock`, and the scope of state handling after withdrawal. Until these two items and the opposite-case inputs have all been recorded, continue to understand the compatibility directory in terms of the old entry point.

# Quality Signal Console: Alternative Approach Proposal

The previous version favored splitting out the control plane because the two failure exits on the existing path in `Orquesta` differ. That assessment is still only a hypothesis: it suggests that an aggregate green result may hide differences in the sources of failure samples, not that splitting will necessarily improve regression attribution.

The proposal is to run a short-term comparison. Keep the original Quality Signal Console entry point, while also having the candidate workflow context retain failure samples from the same batch of tests and fixtures. Both paths will use the same inputs and observation window; record the first failure observed, whether it is subsequently assigned to the same layer, and whether investigation requires repeatedly returning to the raw output. The candidate path will not take over the official entry point.

This comparison changes only where signals are stored. Do not also change test organization, fixture contents, or failure labels; otherwise the results cannot show which part the problem comes from. A single passing run does not count as a result; neither does a tidier display. There needs to be at least one input that contradicts the original assessment: it should cause the original and candidate entry points to produce different failure attributions, so we can tell whether "the two exits differ" has any practical impact.

The case against splitting should also be retained. The original entry point can already collect failure samples; adding another context path would require investigators to first decide which side to look at. If the candidate records cannot point to fixture or test sooner than the original entry point, splitting only increases the maintenance surface area. Rollback is another cost: if the new path has written regression-layering records, withdrawing it requires more than just deleting the display-layer entry point; we also need to confirm that the original entry point still works independently.

The tentative rollback criteria are: no improvement in the time to pinpoint the source, no reduction in misclassifications, or the candidate path requiring changes to existing interfaces to continue. If any one is met, stop the trial and restore the old entry point. After restoration, keep only the raw samples; do not turn hypotheses from the trial into long-term rules.

The current callers of release evidence still haven't been identified. No maintainer has been confirmed either, so this proposal does not set a rollout sequence; it only records the samples to observe and the exit points.

# Quality Signal Dashboard: Alternative Approach Proposal

This draft preserves the original preference for a split and notes the evidence that had not been found at the time. It did not become the execution plan for the Quality Signal Dashboard; the original comparison process can still explain why some people later discussed failure samples and regression tiering separately.

## Original assessment: split out the control plane

The initial idea was straightforward: the Quality Signal Dashboard would continue collecting failure samples from tests and fixtures, but would no longer funnel every sample through the same `Orquesta` aggregation output. The candidate approach was to store workflow context in addition to the existing processing and have a separate control plane handle attribution and tiering.

At the time, the only support for the split was one localized observation: the two failure exit points described in `docs/adj-st2common/proposals/unadopted-st2common-quality-signal-board-approach.md` differed. That difference was interpreted as "a single aggregated result may mask the source," leading to a preference for splitting out the control plane. This draft does not supply the call records that were missing at the time or recast that preference as a validated conclusion.

The assessment in the original draft was: if a failure first appeared on the test side and was then repackaged on the fixture side, a unified entry point could easily retain only the last visible signal. After a split, investigators could first establish which side a sample came from, then decide whether to include it in regression tiering. This sounded reasonable, but at the time there was no proof that all failures passed through both exit points, or that the existing entry point could not retain enough source information.

## Proposed short-term comparison

The second version did not call for replacing the production entry point; it only proposed keeping the old path and adding a candidate record. The comparison inputs were to come from existing tests and fixtures; both paths were to receive the same batch of samples within the same observation window. The planned records included: the failure first observed, which tier that failure ultimately landed in, and whether investigation required revisiting the raw output.

The point was not to have the candidate path generate more records, but to see whether it changed attribution. If both paths could ultimately say only "failure," the candidate path would offer no new basis for judgment even with extra workflow context. Only if a fixture sample was folded into a generic failure on the old path but could be distinguished from the corresponding test on the candidate path would it be worth further discussion of whether tiering was useful.

The original draft called for including a counterexample input. This requirement was not developed into a full experiment plan: it was only a reminder not to choose just the failure samples most likely to support the split. A counterexample might show that, although the two exit points differed, they made no difference to the final attribution; it might also show that the old entry point already retained enough information. Either outcome would weaken the assumption that "splitting it out makes investigation easier."

To avoid distorting the comparison, fixture content, test organization, and failure labels should not be changed at the same time during the trial. If those changes happened together, no green or red result could be attributed to workflow context or the control plane split. The original proposal did not count a clearer presentation layer as success either: display labels could become tidier without reducing misjudgments.

## Objections at the time

The objections were mainly about maintenance. The original entry point already collected failure samples; adding another path would force investigators to decide first whether to look at the old entry point or the candidate one. If the candidate records could not indicate earlier whether a sample came from a test or a fixture, the split would just add another choice.

Another issue was rollback. If the candidate path took part in writing regression-tier data, backing out would require more than removing an entry point; the original entry point would still have to be able to retain the raw failure samples independently. The original draft did not list specific migration steps, because even the existing callers of release evidence had not been confirmed. With that gap, "split it out, then restore it" was still a verbal condition at the time, not an actionable commitment.

Someone had suggested first converting all failures in the Quality Signal Dashboard to the same format, then discussing tiering. That suggestion was not included in the candidate approach: standardizing the format would change both the representation of the inputs and where they were stored, so it would not establish whether the problem lay in the failure exit points or in the format itself. Heterogeneous samples were kept to compare sources, not to prove that they inherently ought to be split into two systems.

## Stop conditions remain as in the old draft

Stop if the candidate records do not identify test or fixture as the source earlier than the original entry point does. Stop if the number of misjudgments does not decrease. Also stop if maintaining the candidate path requires crossing existing interface boundaries. After stopping, restore the old entry point and retain the raw samples from the trial; do not turn a candidate attribution into the official definition of a failure.

These stop conditions do not mean the split has already been reviewed. They merely defined when to back out of the preferred approach at the time. The original draft used "speed of identifying the source" and "number of misjudgments" as observation metrics, but did not define a counting method or confirm who was responsible for judging whether attribution was consistent between the two paths. This was one of the practical constraints that kept the proposal from moving forward.

## Handoff addendum

The handoff entry-point additions were later recorded at ST2C-011. That card first showed a capacity review, followed by the start of work to fill in maintenance entry-point information; these actions did not provide failure samples for the comparison above, nor can they retrospectively prove that the split approach was effective. The callers of release evidence are still left blank in this draft.

This page is being kept not to recommend restarting the split, but to avoid erasing the objections raised at the time: the availability of the old entry point, the differences between fixture and test sources, and the records that regression tiering might leave behind when backing out were all constraints on the proposal. If a new proposal is drawn up later, it should be reassessed using the raw samples and actual call relationships, rather than taking the preference expressed here as a premise.
