# Runtime Observability Console Entry Migration Notes

After this handoff, keep the index split into the old entry, the replacement location, and callers still in use. The logging and trace signals, incident context, and recovery observation window are in the same project, but they should not be merged into a single migration record just because their names are similar.

The previous version's approach was to inspect the directory first, then decide whether the old entry could be retired. That order is retained here so the decision can be reviewed later; it did not solve the problem of callers still reading from the old location. Each move now starts with the incident context retained at the original entry, rather than with the daily report or summary chart.

```text
Old entry
  ├─ logging signals
  ├─ trace fragments
  ├─ incident context
  └─ recovery observation window
        │
        └─ Select one caller still in use
               │
               ├─ Same-window record retained at replacement location: continue
               └─ Record missing or inconsistent: fall back to old entry
```

### Migration Sequence

1. In the old entry, mark the objects to inspect in this batch, retaining the original input, version, and first visible signal.
2. Select only one caller to move to the replacement location. Compare adjacent revisions only at the first path difference; do not include later directory changes in this batch.
3. Keep the old entry readable. When a signal appears at the replacement location, first check whether it still belongs to the same incident context and recovery observation window.
4. After the collection strategy has changed, trends before and after retiring the entry cannot be compared directly. Keep this limitation here; do not use the two curve segments from before and after in place of a same-window check.
5. If the failure sample supplied by the caller is missing, stop the batch at the old entry; do not delete navigation or announce completion.

ST2D-008 The only handoff recorded is the temporary one for this action; the long-term maintainer is still missing from the index. ST2D-010 The adjacent-revision comparison for this range is suitable for confirming the first path difference, but not for proving that the entire call chain has been migrated.

### Recorded Discrepancies

The daily report once merged two execution records, but the original cards had no corresponding merged content. If the daily report is all that can be found later, that alone is not enough to conclude that the trace and logging records came from the same incident; go back to the original location retained at the old entry. This made the earlier wording, "continue as soon as it is visible at the replacement location," too optimistic; it has now been changed to confirm the same consumer and the same observation window first.

### Return to the Old Entry

When reverting, first remove this batch's callers' dependency on the replacement location; continue querying the same objects through the old entry. Do not fabricate an incident context that no longer exists; retain only the logging, trace, and recovery observations that were visible at the time. # Runtime Observability Console Entry Point Migration Guide

This index preserves part of an earlier migration trail for the Runtime Observability Console: the old entry point contains logging, trace, incident contexts, and recovery observation windows; replacement locations take over some of these in batches. It was originally updated as navigation was reorganized, and was later used to follow up on which callers had not yet left the old entry point, so the page contains operational instructions, assessments of what is outdated, and incomplete caller fields.

The earliest criterion treated "a replacement location already exists in the directory" as the sign that migration had begun. This criterion is still retained in the old records because it explains why navigation was cleaned up first at the time; however, it is no longer sufficient to determine whether consumers have moved. In particular, after changes to the collection policy for runtime signals, trends before and after may look the same even though the records are not from the same observation window.

The index file has always been located at `docs/adj-st2api/migration/current-entry-point-legacy-entry-point-migration-index.md`. The entries here cover only st2api-operations-observability: runtime signals built around logging and trace, incident contexts, and recovery observation windows. It has its own schedule, maintainers, and exit criteria; directories from neighboring projects are not used as a basis for filling in this index.

## Reading Conventions Carried Over from the Old Index

The old entry point is not a single address that has already become invalid, but a common starting point for several types of incident records. During the first migration, consumers typically started investigating with one type of signal, then returned to the incident context to cross-check. The old organization grouped these objects together to make it easier to review them by incident context; the cost was that later readers could easily assume they necessarily migrated in the same batch.

The notes at the time had a simplified rule: if the old entry point opens and the replacement location also opens, keep proceeding. This rule was later retained with a correction added. Both locations being readable only means the navigation still exists; it does not mean the caller has switched, nor does it mean the two locations retain signals from the same run.

```text
Old entry point
  ├── logging signals
  ├── trace fragments
  ├── Incident context
  └── Recovery observation window
          │
          ├── Caller selected for this batch
          │       │
          │       └── Replacement location
          │
          └── Unconfirmed callers still query through the old entry point
```

The branches in the diagram show the record sequence, not the service topology. While the old entry point still exists, first use the original input, version, and first signal it preserved as the source of truth. A replacement location counts as the follow-on location for this batch only if it can be linked to the same caller and the same observation window.

## Earlier Assessments for the First Migration Batch

Early records treated logging and trace as objects that could be moved together. This was to reduce duplicate navigation, not because it had been confirmed that both were consumed by the same consumer. This assessment was not later removed from the page because existing old links still point to it; when reading this section now, treat it as the organizational approach used at the time, and do not use it to expand the migration scope.

The old records also assumed that rollback only required restoring the old entry point. This approach could still be used when the original incident context was available to consult, but it did not handle cases where trial records had already been left at the replacement location. Later batches therefore changed the procedure: before restoring the old entry point, first mark which records exist only at the replacement location; after restoration, retain these records as a trial batch rather than mixing them back into the historical portion of the old entry point.

The caller fields were incomplete in the first version. This was not because all callers had already migrated away, but because only the entry point and replacement location had been confirmed at the time. This gap remains. During directory cleanup, "no callers registered" must not be used to infer "no callers".

## Sequence for Moving in Batches

Each batch handles only one caller that is still in use. First retrieve from the old entry point the objects that need to be checked for this batch: the relevant logging or trace signals, the corresponding incident context, and the first visible result in the recovery observation window. When recording these objects, there is no need to copy the entire history again to the replacement location; what matters is that it remains possible to tell later that they came from the same batch.

Next, change only one condition: have that caller read or write records through the replacement location. The old entry point remains readable at this stage. Once content appears at the replacement location, check the original input, version, first visible signal, and the status of the second query. Aggregated or organized views can help locate information, but cannot replace the original location.

When comparing adjacent current revision entries, look only at the first path difference. This restriction came from a check of adjacent links: if subsequent directory changes, collection changes, or changes to other pages are all included in the same comparison, the result cannot show exactly which change altered the entry point. ST2D-010 are retained as navigation for this comparison.

A batch stays at the old entry point in the following cases: the replacement location has no records from the same window; the caller cannot provide a failure sample; the relationship between trace and logging can only be inferred by working backward from daily reports; or the recovery observation window has already spanned a collection policy change. Stopping does not mean deleting trial records; trial records should retain their batch context.

## Notes Added After the Collection Policy Change

This section was added after the original index. After the collection policy changed, trends before and after moving off the entry point cannot be compared directly. The old version treated a flattening trend as a sign that the switchover was stable; this claim was later overturned because the collection policy itself changes the shape of the visible signals.

Therefore, when trends differ, first ask whether they come from the same recovery observation window, then ask whether the caller has switched to the replacement location. If neither can be confirmed, retain the old entry point and mark the replacement location as pending verification. Do not splice trace data from different windows into a single record just to produce a continuous chart.

The daily report merged two execution records, while the original card did not contain this merged content. This means that the daily report cannot serve as migration evidence on its own: it may compress two incident contexts into a single result, or obscure the first signal retained only at the old entry point. ST2D-009 relate to outdated navigation cleanup; the cleanup cannot supply records that were not in the original card.

## Restoring the Old Path

When records at the replacement location are missing or inconsistent, or the caller cannot provide a failure sample, first undo this batch's switchover and have the caller work through the old entry point again. Do not backfill the original input, version, or first visible result at the old entry point; recovery observations should record only what can actually still be seen after restoration.

If trial records have already been generated at the replacement location, do not delete them or rewrite them as history from the old entry point. Keep an indication of "trial batch" beside the entry so that later investigations do not mistake trace data generated after migration for the old incident context. This handling corrects the old version's "restoration means overwriting" approach.

After restoration, check the same caller's query status at least once more. The point is not whether the trend looks good, but whether the old entry point can still provide records for the original objects. If the old entry point itself no longer has the corresponding incident context, the index must not describe it as restorable; keep the item marked as outdated and wait for the caller to provide additional material.

## Checks Before Leaving the Old Entry Point

The old entry point is removed from a batch's path only after that batch meets the following conditions: the replacement location can handle the corresponding objects; the actual caller confirms it has moved; historical queries can still find the pre-migration incident context. If any of the three is missing, retain the old entry point.

For logging and trace, confirmation does not require both to be moved at the same time. They may belong to different callers or different recovery observation windows. Recording them separately preserves the provenance of the old incident context better than forcing a single completion date.

Incident contexts and recovery observation windows are also not considered complete based on "the page has been updated". For incident contexts, it must be possible to return to the first visible record; for recovery observation windows, it must be clear which batch is being observed after the switchover. Without this material, the index should still say "unconfirmed" rather than changing empty fields to migrated.

ST2D-008 document only temporary takeovers; long-term maintainers were not automatically determined as a result. When entry point cleanup is involved, first follow the existing maintenance records in the index for that batch's objects; keep entries without maintenance records on the old path, and do not substitute a temporary takeover for long-term ownership.

## Sections That Are Still Outdated

The old index's statement that "rollback is possible as soon as the replacement location is readable" no longer applies; the original text has not been deleted so that it can explain why the old navigation was cleaned up. The old index's implicit practice that "daily reports can stand in for the incident context" also no longer applies; daily reports are only suitable for helping locate information and cannot replace records at the old entry point.

Another old explanation calls all remaining callers a single batch. This passage has no supporting evidence and is retained as outdated. When adding callers later, group them into batches by their actual usage locations rather than merging consumers with similar names.

Items still incomplete: which callers still rely on the old entry point; how long querying through the old entry point remains available after rollback; whether the replacement location's handling of missing trace data needs to be documented separately. These questions cannot be answered from the existing navigation and daily reports.

DOC-42 record the maintainer mapping; the focus here remains on migration traces for the old entry point, replacement locations, and callers.

# Runtime Observability Console Maintainer Map

Consumers, the index, and exit actions all reference the record for `st2api-operations-observability`. This map separates the issue intake contacts from the people who can make technical determinations; temporary coverage is also listed separately, so a single integration-debugging handoff isn't mistakenly recorded as long-term ownership.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A[Consumer or index detects an anomaly] --> B{Can the record revision be identified first?}
    B -- Yes --> C[Runtime Observability Console on-duty contact]
    B -- No --> D[Leave revision unspecified and check the directory]
    C --> E{Which area does the issue fall under?}
    E -- Runtime signals or entry points --> F[On-duty contact triages the issue]
    E -- Exit actions --> G[Relevant module maintainer]
    E -- Temporary coverage --> H[Assignee at the integration debugging session]
    F --> I{Is a technical determination needed?}
    I -- Yes --> G
    I -- No --> J[Record symptoms and handoff destination]
```

| Object at issue | First point of contact | What they can handle | Who makes technical determinations long-term |
|---|---|---|---|
| The `st2api-operations-observability` page and its attachments | Runtime Observability Console on-duty contact | Check whether the page, directory, and consumers refer to the same record revision; pass a minimal description of the symptoms to the next area. | The relevant module maintainer; the on-duty contact is not a substitute. |
| Runtime signals from logging and trace | Runtime Observability Console on-duty contact | Record the first signals observed, the record revision, and the indexing timestamp. | The maintainer of the module the signals relate to. |
| Exit actions | Relevant module maintainer | Determine whether the exit entry point still leads to the current record. | The relevant module maintainer. |
| Temporary coverage | Assignee at the integration debugging session | Pick up the handed-off card and session context, and state the extent of their coverage. | The original object's long-term owner; temporary coverage does not change ownership. |
| Long-term ownership of `metrics` |  | Still unconfirmed. | Leave blank; do not infer ownership from whoever replied most recently. |
| release evidence |  | Still unconfirmed. | Leave blank. |

The old diagram placed "Runtime Observability Console on-duty" and "module maintainer" too close together, making it easy in practice to mistake the intake contact for the person responsible for answering. The agreement is now: the on-duty contact is responsible for tying the issue to an inspectable record; only the relevant module maintainer can confirm behavior, scope, or fix trade-offs. Project coordination can arrange a window, but does not give a combined answer on behalf of these two contacts.

When consumers arrive through the directory or a report, check the revision of the referenced record first, then the indexing timestamp. The two `st2api-operations-observability` entries with the same name must not be displayed as one: keep the old link as an old record; it must not overwrite the current record. If the indexing timestamp and event timestamp are out of order, first record the time difference; do not describe it as a content change without material that explains it. ST2D-002, ST2D-003, ST2D-004, and ST2D-005 retain navigation entry points for mixed display, the link chain for the current revision, missing reconstruction material, and indexing-time discrepancies, respectively.

The replay through the exit entry point stopped at step three. This only shows that the flow through that entry point did not complete; it does not justify assigning the exit action to the Runtime Observability Console. Follow this sequence:

1. Record which directory, report, or page was used to enter, and which revision it pointed to at the time.
2. If the interruption at step three can be reproduced, hand off the interruption point and the original entry point to the module maintainer for the exit action.
3. If integration debugging staff are taking over the session, state explicitly in the handoff that this is temporary coverage; do not change the long-term owner in the diagram.
4. If there is no material that can be used to reconstruct what happened, keep the page description hidden or leave it blank; do not fill in a seemingly complete conclusion.

The integration debugging session was previously handed off to a new assignee along with the card, making "who is responding" and "who owns the object" easier to confuse. The temporary-coverage column in the diagram is only for this kind of case: the assignee can continue asking questions, collect logging or trace, and report back where it failed; whether the exit action is effective, or whether a signal represents system state, still needs to be confirmed by the module the object belongs to. When temporary coverage ends, the point of contact reverts to the Runtime Observability Console on-duty contact or the module maintainer; the temporary assignment is not retained as a new long-term entry.

For the page itself, the Runtime Observability Console maintains the entry point and attachments; for technical objects described on the page, maintainers answer separately for each object. For issues spanning multiple areas, the person asking does not need to write up the full session context again; they only need to include the original entry point, record revision, indexing timestamp, and the first visible failure point. This lets the person receiving the issue confirm the routing first, so the technical assessment is not rewritten during the handoff.

The historical issue of the two versions of the record not being merged is still documented in DOC-43. This map does not determine which version's content is correct; it only ensures that the old record, current record, exit actions, and temporary coverage each have a destination.

# Runtime Observability Console Dual-Version Record Review

At one point, the same entry displayed the current records for two revisions simultaneously. The first thing to surface was that the regression did not match the old record: the entry still appeared usable, but the comparison could no longer show which version had been read. At the time, the issue was understood as the record not having been merged, not as the runtime signal itself having failed.

The main impact was on people who relied on this entry to verify historical output. The old record had not disappeared, and the new revision had no separate location of its own, so a single lookup could mix the two contexts. During that period, the result could not be judged from the last line of green output alone; the request context and retained versions had to be reviewed together.

### Timeline

- At initial discovery, it was only confirmed that the regression differed from the old record.
- The follow-up did not keep retrying the entry; instead, it retained the version present at the time in `docs/adj-st2api/incidents/st2api-operations-observability-unmerged-record-versions.md`.
- The handoff added the version, request context, and stop conditions. The review found Mongo state, but this only shows that a state record had been checked at the time; it cannot by itself explain why two versions appeared simultaneously.
- Later, it was confirmed that the workflow context could be restored. This was initially taken as an indication that the entry had recovered, but that judgment was too broad in retrospect: it covered context recovery only, not whether the record consumer would still read a mixed version.

Stopping further retries prevented new observations from being written back into the old entry. The retained file remains the starting point for the investigation that located the issue, and the attachments also remain in the Runtime Observability Console materials; speculation about adjacent services was not recorded here as a cause.

### Unresolved Items

There was no conclusion at the time about why StatsD changed. Nor was the scope of the final remaining use of adj-st2api established; even if there was no consumer, the actual search boundary should have been recorded. ST2D-001, ST2D-011 and ST2D-012 later respectively proposed retracting the old relationship, adding stop conditions, and confirming the final user, but they do not change the timeline of this incident record.

The earlier statement that "two revisions had stably coexisted in the same entry" no longer applies. It described the page state seen at the time and should no longer be treated as proof that recovery was complete.

# Team Shared Entry-Point Maintenance FAQ

Three questions have been kept alongside the shared entry point, originally so that people adding candidate paths would not have to reopen the debate about entry-point checks, withdrawal, and closure every time. Early answers tended to treat the entry point as the center of the assessment; later feedback from the field did not result in this page being taken down, only in changes to the parts that could be confirmed. The text below therefore retains the old approach while also marking where it can no longer be followed.

## What can the existing inquiry-validation entry point prove?

The old answer was: as long as a candidate path could go through the existing entry point, the shared entry point had already provided enough confirmation for the change; any remaining scheduler or workflow issues could wait until the next release cycle. This wording incorrectly turned "can go through a check" into "the cumulative state is already consistent."

The review could confirm only a narrower point: the entry point can support one check, inquiry validation. It cannot replace the negative case, nor can it show that persisted state, scheduler, and workflow already agree with one another. Without a native test transcript, do not fill in an imagined record of a pass; these questions can remain, but the answer should be recorded as unknown.

## Who is responsible for withdrawing candidate paths?

The old answer assigned withdrawal to the shared entry-point maintainer, on the grounds that they maintained the entry point, so candidate paths should also be withdrawn along with it. This answer still explains why some people directly deleted candidate entries at the time, but it did not distinguish between "recording a withdrawal request" and "confirming the scope of withdrawal."

Recent feedback is only sufficient to correct this one point: the entry-point maintainer can record or remove candidate entries at the entry point, but doing so does not make them the person responsible for confirming withdrawal. This page still does not specify who proposes candidate paths or who can confirm their withdrawal. Do not infer from the old answer that any role has already accepted this responsibility.

## What are the conditions for closure?

The old version listed cumulative checks and persisted state together and then allowed closure; in practice, the negative case was often treated as an optional addition. The closure wording the team continued to use at the time was: "Close a change only after the cumulative checks, the negative case, and the persisted state agree, with unresolved scheduler or workflow evidence recorded for the next release." This wording differs from the old answer: the negative case needs to agree with the cumulative checks and persisted state; unresolved scheduler or workflow evidence cannot be papered over with an entry-point check and can only be left for the next release.

# Team Shared Entry Point Maintenance: Decision for This Round

This round compared two approaches: retain the existing runner-compat shared entry point, or adjust the entry point during the maintenance window. The decision was to retain the existing entry point for now. The old entry point remains subject to withdrawal until the conditions for a later switch are met.

The review materials require the actual impact, the coordinator, and the handling of the old entry point to all be recorded at the time of the switch. The maintenance window only identifies a time available for focused work; it does not, by itself, show that the entry-point adjustment is ready to implement.

The immediate-adjustment option was not adopted. The existing materials cover only the maintenance scope that has already been rechecked; if the entry-point change, impact assessment, and withdrawal arrangements were bundled into a single action, it would be hard afterward to distinguish assessments that had been confirmed from ideas considered at the time.

Keeping the entry point does not mean its present form is permanent, nor does it mean stopping preparations for an adjustment. It means maintaining continuity of the shared entry point until the impact description, handoff and acceptance arrangements, and conditions for withdrawing the old entry point have all been clearly documented together. The specific switchover actions are recorded in DOC-52.

versions.body:
# This Round's Maintenance Decision for the Team's Public Entry Point

The public runner-compat entry point will remain in place. Preparations for changing the entry point can continue, but the change will not happen by default simply because a maintenance window becomes available. The initial draft reduced the decision to "leave the entry point unchanged for now." Review found that this wording omitted two conditions that affect subsequent maintenance: why the old entry point should remain, and who will take responsibility for the impact statement and retirement arrangements when the switchover happens.

This addendum addresses only the maintenance trade-offs for the team's public entry point. The runner's directory location, whether individual files are retained, and each caller's usage habits may all provide leads for review, but they are not being reconsidered here. Treating a code location as an entry point decision would make a directory change look like a completed switchover of the public surface; conversely, an opinion about the entry point that is detached from the items actually examined cannot be reviewed either.

## Decision Made

This round retains the current runner-compat public entry point and leaves changing it as an option for which preparations can continue. The current entry point carries forward existing maintenance assessments. Changing the entry point requires a separate, explicit switchover handoff; a maintenance window is merely a period suited to handling the work together, not evidence that the change has been approved.

When preparing to implement a change, the record must document three things together: the actual impact, a coordinator, and an old entry point that can be retired. These three items must not be scattered across disconnected verbal conclusions. If the desired new entry point is known but the effects on existing maintenance assessments cannot be explained, the change does not yet have an assessable scope; if only the impact is documented, with no one taking responsibility, continuity in the maintenance record will break after the change; if the new entry point is already present but there are no conditions for retiring the old one, temporary retention will become an unbounded compatibility burden.

Therefore, if any of the three items is missing, the public entry point remains unchanged. Materials can still be organized, maintenance windows discussed, and existing check results verified, but these preparations do not amount to a change that has already occurred on the public surface. This stopping point applies only to the public entry point switchover; it does not require mapping calls to every runner before each maintenance activity.

Retaining the current entry point is not a vote against future changes either. What can be confirmed at this stage is entry point continuity, not a fully explained migration. If a future switchover handoff can explain the impact, coordination responsibilities, and conditions for retiring the old entry point, the two approaches can still be compared again.

## Approaches Compared at the Time

The first approach was to maintain the existing runner-compat entry point and keep the maintenance work that could already be reviewed this round within the current public surface. This would not require moving existing maintenance assessments together with an entry point change whose full impact had not yet been explained. Those who come later would still be able to use the same entry point to look back at the trade-offs recorded this round.

This does not mean the old entry point has no cost. As long as it remains, there is still a compatibility burden; it will still be necessary to determine when it can be retired and connect new materials to the existing record. Choosing to retain it means not disguising a switchover assessment that has not yet been worked out as a completed cleanup.

The second approach was to change the entry point during a maintenance window. Its appeal was that the entry point's form, the handoff, and subsequent maintenance appeared to be manageable together. But the meeting materials explicitly required documenting the actual impact, a coordinator, and an old entry point that could be retired. Replacing those details with "the window is here" would mistake a convenient time to schedule work for a basis for implementation.

A change window answers when the work can be handled together; it cannot answer which existing maintenance assessments will be affected. Nor does it automatically specify the conditions under which the old entry point should remain, or who will follow through on the changes after the switchover. When the entry point changes first and the record is filled in later, those who come afterward see only that the new entry point exists and cannot determine whether a narrower, more easily reversible option was available at the time.

For that reason, this round did not approve the second approach as the default action. The possibility of changing the entry point later was not rejected; what was rejected was bundling the change, impact assessment, and handling of the old entry point into a change that had not yet been fully explained. This distinction must be preserved so that a maintenance window is not later misread as advance authorization for an entry point change.

## Materials Used for Review

This round's review started with runner-related entry points and call names near `st2common/st2common/runners/utils.py`. That location can help those who come later return to the items discussed at the time, but it does not specify the permanent home of the public entry point. A change in file location does not by itself prove that entry point migration is complete, nor can it replace the handoff details that must be added at switchover.

The assessment standard retained during review was:

> Every control-plane claim is tied to a reproducible repository path, an observable boundary, and the release evidence that lets the next maintainer challenge it.

This sentence has a specific role in this decision. An entry point assessment included in release materials should be traceable to a repository path, an inspectable behavioral boundary, and the corresponding release materials. It does not require every possible call to be listed here, nor does it allow unexamined areas to be presented as a complete impact analysis.

What was approved this round was the maintenance scope supported by existing materials, not a reorganization covering every way runners are used. Partial materials with established correspondences can support partial assessments; a path or call name alone does not automatically establish that the impact of changing the entry point is clear.

The initial draft treated "having release materials" too much like a sufficient condition. The understanding after review is that release materials can establish only what they actually cover, and that coverage must correspond to the paths and behavioral boundaries examined at the time. The absence of a complete map does not invalidate partial checks, but partial checks must not be expanded into comprehensive conclusions either.

Code locations, call names, and check results are one type of record: they help people find the items examined at the time; the trade-offs involved in retaining, changing, or retiring an entry point are another type of record: they explain why the public surface remained unchanged at that point in time. The former can serve as a starting point for review, but cannot replace the latter. If the latter is detached from the former, it also becomes an abstract opinion that cannot be questioned meaningfully.

## Relationships to Preserve at Switchover

Actual impact is not simply "this will affect downstream." The switchover record needs to explain which maintenance items handled through the current public entry point have been covered by this assessment; which existing assessments the entry point change will carry into the handoff; and which unfinished arrangements would lose their buffer if the old entry point were retired. If the materials cover only part of the scope, retain that part as such: do not describe the gaps as having no impact, and do not automatically expand those gaps into a requirement to migrate every usage pattern.

The impact statement should precede the change, rather than being added as an explanation after the entry point changes. If the change happens first and the record is backfilled afterward, the record can easily be reduced to the fact that the new entry point already exists, without the basis for believing at the time that it could replace the old one. The continuity of the public entry point depends precisely on this assessment being available for later review.

This round did not turn "callers need a stable entry point" into a permanent compatibility commitment. The current choice has a narrower meaning: when there is insufficient information to explain the impact of a change, do not carry existing maintenance assessments into a migration that happens by default. As more materials become available, a new decision can narrow or change the scope of retention; this handling must not be retroactively treated as a promise made at the time never to change the entry point.

The impact record does not need to strive for comprehensive wording. It needs to let those participating in the switchover distinguish confirmed items, items that need to be handed over, and items that remain unconfirmed. Combining all three into a general risk description neither helps determine whether the old entry point can still be retired nor tells the coordinator which part needs to be filled in next.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[Existing runner-compat public entry point] --> B{Is the switchover record complete}
    B -->|No| C[Retain the current entry point]
    B -->|Yes| D[Prepare the switchover handoff]
    D --> E[Actual impact]
    D --> F[Coordinator]
    D --> G[Old entry point that can be retired]
    E --> H[Reassess the entry point change]
    F --> H
    G --> H
    H --> I[Change it or continue to retain it]
```

The three items in the diagram are not three sequential procedures. They describe relationships that must hold at the same time for a single change: the impact determines what can be clearly established about the change, the coordinator takes responsibility for the records and changes, and the old entry point provides a buffer while remaining subject to retirement. If any one of these is missing, the change should not be recorded as complete.

The coordinator is not a standing title detached from a specific change. In an actual switchover, someone needs to connect the maintenance records, known impact, and release materials: why the old entry point is being retained temporarily, what actually changed during the change window, and who will bring the retirement arrangements back into discussion when the assessment changes. Without this continuity of responsibility, even if the entry point has changed, the record will end at an operation with no follow-up.

No permanent person was designated this round. Fixing a name does not automatically produce handoff details and may instead lead those who come later to assume that entry point maintenance inherently belongs to a particular role. What is confirmed here is that the coordination responsibility cannot be left unassigned; who specifically takes it on should be documented in the switchover record according to the actual scope of that change.

Coordination after the switchover also cannot make up for an assessment missing before implementation. The coordinator can organize materials, follow through on known issues, and arrange the handling of the old entry point, but cannot turn a missing impact statement into a basis that already existed. If the impact and retirement conditions have not yet been established, the coordinator is taking responsibility only for a change that has already happened, not for a change that is still open to choice.

## Position on Retaining the Old Entry Point

An old entry point that can be retired does not mean maintaining two equivalent approaches over the long term. It means that while the impact assessment for the new entry point may still change, the old entry point remains as an explicit buffer. Before retirement conditions have been established, it cannot simply be deleted as an unowned leftover; at the same time, its continued presence must not be taken to mean that it will exist indefinitely.

The argument for immediately cleaning up the old entry point is that fewer entry points make maintenance more focused. That argument does not address the timing gap during switchover: existing maintenance materials may still use the old entry point as a reference, and known impacts may still be getting added to the switchover record. Removing the entry point first and filling in the handoff later reduces only the apparent number of entry points, while leaving an unexplained gap in the assessment.

Another arrangement that was not adopted was retaining the old entry point without documenting retirement conditions and waiting for it to disappear naturally through maintenance. That would turn temporary retention into an unbounded compatibility state. Subsequent maintainers would be unable either to explain why it remained or to determine whether new materials were sufficient to support retirement. The number of entry points would not actually have decreased; only the basis for handling them would have been lost.

Retirement conditions also cannot be stated merely as "confirm no impact." That wording does not identify what is to be confirmed and cannot be checked against the actual handoff. The conditions should be connected to the known impacts and responsibility relationships in the record for that change, allowing people to determine whether the reasons for temporary retention still hold. The current materials do not provide a generalizable checklist of conditions, so none is being invented here.

## Division of Responsibilities with the Switchover Handoff

The long-term form of the entry point after a change was not decided this round. The current conclusion requires only that the old entry point remain until its retirement conditions are met, and that changing the entry point not be the default action before an impact statement and coordination responsibilities are established. It does not prescribe a new name that must be used in the future, nor does it prescribe how runner directories should be arranged.

The full scope of call impacts was not collected here either. At the actual switchover, the impacts known at that time and the areas still awaiting confirmation should be recorded, rather than expanding partial checks into conclusions about all callers. Conversely, the absence of a complete list should not be used to omit maintenance facts that have already been confirmed.

DOC-52 handles the specific switchover handoff. This record preserves the trade-offs between the two approaches, the reasons an immediate change was not approved, and the requirement that retiring the old entry point remain possible. If new materials expand the known scope, that handoff should be updated; this round's decision should not be read backward as though the full picture had already been known at the time.

This decision is being retained so that when a change is proposed again later, the reasons for not treating a maintenance window as a basis for implementation at the time will still be visible. New materials can support a new entry point assessment; the availability of a maintenance window alone is not enough to change this round's choice to preserve public entry point continuity.

# Shared Entry Point Cutover Handoff Notes

This handoff covers maintenance of the team's shared entry point, not relocation of a single file. The old entry point remains the reference for the pre-cutover state; a candidate path can replace it only after the known consumers have been accounted for and someone has actually tried it and can roll back. api-client is the subject of the handoff. `st2client/st2client/models/trace.py` is retained only as a record of one lookup and cannot establish the entry point's permanent home.

## Record the full state first

At the start of the cutover, the record should answer at least four questions: which entry point is still in use; which consumers have been found; what the candidate path is; and which consumer Fang Ke can roll back on its own. Do not equate "searched for call names" with "all consumers accounted for." Do not record just a single green result, either. The handoff needs a minimal counterexample: if a known consumer can still use only the old entry point, or there is no actionable rollback step after the trial, the migration is still in progress.

The lookup in the early records led to `st2client/st2client/models/trace.py`. A later review retained that trail while moving the question back from "where is the file?" to "who uses the team's shared entry point, and who can provide confirmation after the cutover?" Files can help locate call names; they cannot replace a consumer list.

## Cutover sequence

1. **List the old entry point.** Start by recording the name of the entry point in use and the consumers that can still be confirmed. Leave unknowns blank; do not fill them in with the candidate path.
2. **Check the candidate path.** Let consumers that can roll back on their own try it first. The trial record needs to include the consumer, the path actually taken, and the state on return; "verified" alone is not enough.
3. **Keep a rollback point.** During the trial, the old entry point remains the recovery path. On failure, first roll back the consumer's switch, then add the failure symptoms to the handoff record. Without a rollback action, do not move on to the next batch.
4. **Hand off to the next boundary.** Hand the trial results to the owner who can confirm that boundary. This person does not need to vouch for every caller, only to confirm this segment between the current consumer and the candidate path.
5. **Then handle the remaining consumers.** Move the remaining consumers from the old entry point to the candidate path only when both the list and rollback actions exist. If either is missing, stop at this batch.

The state can be recorded in this form:

```text
Known consumers ──check──> Candidate path ──trial──> Reversible result
     │                                 │                              │
     └──still on old entry point───────┴──roll back on failure────────┘
```

## Minimum contents of the handoff record

| Item | What to record |
| --- | --- |
| Old entry point | The entry point actually used before the cutover, not a presumed permanent location |
| Known consumers | Confirmed consumers of api-client; list unconfirmed consumers separately |
| Candidate path | The entry point being tried in this batch |
| Trial consumer | The consumer that can roll back on its own |
| Observed result | Which path was taken, whether it returned to a usable state, and what the failure symptoms were |
| Rollback | The rollback action performed on failure; mark incomplete if there is no action |
| Confirmation boundary | The owner who can confirm whether this segment of the migration is valid |

"Known" has a specific scope here: it means only the consumers found during this handoff that can be rechecked, not that the full scope of api-client usage has been accounted for. If the consumer list is missing, add the list first; if the rollback action is missing, add the action first. Do not substitute the entry point file's location, call-name search results, or an aggregate status for either.

## How to record an in-progress migration

The handoff can pause after the candidate path has been tried. Keep the old entry point as a rollback point and record the reason for stopping. If a consumer is known to exist but its ability to roll back on its own is unknown, record "consumer known, rollback unconfirmed"; if the path has been tried but no actual result was recorded, record "path tried, result not recorded." Neither state can be marked complete.

The assessment on this page remains: `A handoff names the current state, the smallest counterexample, and the owner who can confirm the next boundary; it never substitutes a green summary for an absent trace.` Therefore, at the next handoff, add the minimal counterexample and the corresponding owner first, then decide whether to proceed to the next batch. There is not yet enough evidence to confirm that all consumers have completed the cutover, so the record of the old entry point and candidate path coexisting is retained.

# Cumulative control-plane compatibility surfaces

Revision: quality-repair-072-20260926-v1. This public page lists callable names,
argument envelopes, and module navigation. Detailed behavior, branch precedence,
persistence/re-read rules, timing, and exact error text remain in the routed owner
facts and fixed follow-up gates. Local import aliases and helper decomposition are
not contracts.

## Public workflow entry points

The workflow service exposes these callable boundaries:

- `st2common.services.workflows.is_action_execution_under_workflow_context(execution)`
  accepts an execution object with a context mapping.
- `workflows.inspect_task_contents(spec)` accepts a workflow specification and
  returns structured content diagnostics.
- `st2actions.workflows.workflows.WorkflowExecutionHandler.process(message)`
  processes a workflow message and has a structured error path for unsupported
  messages.
- `workflows.request_resume(action_execution)` accepts an action execution.
- `workflows.request(definition, action_execution, st2_context, notify_cfg=None)`
  accepts a definition, action execution, context mapping, and optional notification
  configuration and returns the workflow execution record. The action execution
  supplies `id`, `action.ref`, `parameters`, and `context`; `st2_context` contains
  an `st2` mapping.
- `workflows.request_next_tasks(workflow_execution, task_ex_id=None)` accepts a
  workflow execution and optional task execution identifier.
- `workflows.request_task_execution(workflow_execution, st2_context, task_request)`
  accepts a task request envelope and returns its task execution record. The request
  envelope may carry task identity, route, specification, context, actions, delay,
  item count, and concurrency; itemized action requests may carry an item identifier.
  The specification object supplies `name`, `action`, `serialize()`, and
  `has_items()`; action requests carry `action`, `input`, and itemized `item_id`.
